It's not so often that the ending of a book has annoyed me this much. Usually if I don't like a book, but don't hate it enough to make me want to put it down instantly, I'll continue till the end. The ending is most often the best part of the book, and it will give satisfaction once it's all over. Nothing like that for The Rose Throne. That's seriously one of the most unsatisfactory endings I have ever seen. 
 Ailsbeth and Marissa are both princesses, but their worlds couldn't be different. Each belonging to one country, both countries separated by the sea and only connected by one bridge. Ailsbeth lives in a dangerous court with an insane king leading it, and she's born with the wrong kind of magic, the male kind. Marissa has a loving father and her country is peaceful, but since her mother passed away she has responsibilities fit for a queen. Their lives are bound together by a prophecy - one day their lands will be one. 
 I don't know what this book was going for. Bitter-sweet romance? Political intruige? Fantasy dystopian? I see traces of all of these, but none of them is completely fleshed out. The characters, the events... All of them are told in the same lack-lustre manner that kept me from connecting with any of them. 
 The world Ms Harrison creates is interesting, but lacks depth. I suspect she's holding out on details so she can throw them at us in later instalments of the series, but for me this doesn't work. There is a serious lack of explanations going on. From the start of the story you are thrown into a world with weyr, unweyrs, taweyr, neweyr and Weirwood. I don't know about you, but from this I kind of pictured weyr to be a kind of tree. It took me quite a while to figure out that weyr is a kind of magic, because nowhere it is explained. Taweyr is the male, destruction kind of magic, and neweyr is the nature-y female kind of magic. Well colour me surprised, the females have nursing magic and males war magic? Baw-ring. There is also a third kind, ekhono who have the wrong kind of magic. 
 Throughout the book almost all the characters talk about is the fate of the kingdoms, of what will happen and how everyone is in danger. Well, at the end of the book NOTHING is different than there is at the start. Why would you make us worry so much about something you aren't even going to use? The characters are inconsistent and confused, one moment they are childish or selfish, the other moment they go on and on about their duty towards their country, sometimes even in the same paragraph. 
 I think The Rose Throne is going for a kind of gruesome princess-story, because there are dozens of executions and poisonings. Almost every few chapters someone's dying, and she even kills off some main characters effortlessly. I get that you don't want your story to be like a fairy-tale, but this went a bit out of bounds. You can't make us feel for a character, than kill him off towards the end without any drama surrounding it. There is no emotional shock, only a confused "...huh?". It might work for GRR Martin, but I don't think it worked in The Rose Throne. 
 This is not a book I will remember fondly, not an author I'll read again. I only recommend The Rose Throne if you have the rest of the series nearby, because on its own it's not a satisfying read.

 I haven't read a Colleen Hoover book since Finding Cinderella was released, so I figured it was time to catch up. I put holds on every audiobook the library had of her books, and this was the first one to come available. I didn't even read the synopsis, just started listening. 
 First thing first, this book broke me. At first I thought Miles was just a jerk who was throwing a fit because his ickle heart was hurted when he was a teenager. Oh no. I wish that's what happened. Because then I wouldn't have spent a good portion of today sobbing. 
 There was one point when everything clicked into place. I was working on a project for the blog while listening. My kid walked into the room, very confused as to why I was crying over a spreadsheet. 
 When it comes to the narration, Grace Grant was great. I had no issues. Deacon Lee, on the other hand, reminded me of Steve Buscemi. It was harder to take him seriously. 
 In conclusion, I can't believe I went this long without reading a Colleen Hoover book. She is incredibly talented and awesome. I'm looking forward to reading every single one of her books, because I must.

Having read American Gods by Neil Gaiman I was a bit hesitant to read The Ocean at the End of the Lane. Why? Because I have mixed feelings about American Gods. On one side, it's brilliant and imaginative, on another it's dark and disturbing (don't get me wrong, I like dark, AG just pushed it to a different level). A friend of mine talked me into reading The Ocean at the End of the Lane so I gave it a go. It wasn't quite what I expected. Yes, a bit dark and disturbing at times, but overall mysterious and magical. I get the impression that this story sits closely to Neil Gaiman's heart, having originally been intended as a short story. The characters are imaginative and well thought-out, the story mystifying and intriguing. The thoughts and ideas of the protagonist fit well for a young boy, and I liked how Gaiman gave a fantasy to a lover of fantasy books. This is a dark fantasy with a 9-year-old protagonist, but I would say the book is geared more toward adults than youth. Also, those who are sensitive about views of creation should take note that, even though this is a fantasy, Gaiman pushes a very unbiblical idea. Overall, a good read.

04/18/2016: This book just won this year's Pulitzer Prize Award for Fiction. Well deserved. 
 for plot, etc., click here to get to my reading journal. Otherwise, carry on. 
 The narrator of this novel, the titular "sympathizer," is definitely a "man of two faces," and faces a number of contradictions. In fact, this thought-provoking novel is so filled with contradictions that this "two faces" idea runs throughout the book. In the narrator's case, he is a man of mixed parentage, a fact that has helped to define his identity throughout his life, since in Vietnam, he grew up being reminded that he is a bastard, with a French father and Vietnamese mother. Metaphorically speaking then, he already understands what is implied in belonging in two different places, but the truth is that he is also not in a position to claim either as his. This idea is repeated again and again throughout the novel, and is one of the main thematic issues explored here, as is the reinvention of the self under less-than-perfect circumstances. He finds himself with different and often-conflicting loyalties, and above all, he is haunted by ghosts. It is truly a masterpiece of a novel that also examines not only American perceptions of the Vietnam War, but America's perception of itself in the war and those of the Vietnamese people as well. 
 I read a reader response of The Sympathizer that said it should be required reading for every US politician, a sentiment I heartily endorse, especially considering what's going on in the world regarding refugees right now. But there's so much more here -- it is a novel just filled with contradictions which make for a great satirical look at the promises of the American dream, at America's place in the world, etc.; it also points out among other things that unlike most historical accounts, the history of the Vietnam war has been the provenance of the losers rather than that of the victors. It also examines the realities behind revolutions and the effects of the postwar diaspora from the point of view of the people who were given promises that were never intended to be kept. 
 A couple of things: first, when I finished it, I sat in my chair absolutely stunned for probably about half an hour. I noted somewhere that even after it was over my jaw was still pinned to the floor; it took me a day or two to get over that feeling. Second, I want to throttle the dustjacket blurber who says this is a "gripping spy novel" -- people who decide to read this book based on that phrase are bound to be somewhat disappointed since this book goes well beyond the boundaries of a mere spy novel. Third, The Sympathizer is one of the most original books I've read this year, well deserving of any award its author receives. I have been very frustrated lately and at the point of despairing over "same old, same old" in recent novels. There are exceptions, of course, including but not necessarily limited to three of my favorite books this year -- A Brief History of Seven Killings, The Buried Giant, and a book published by Pushkin by Peter Froberg Idling called Song for an Approaching Storm about Pol Pot in his pre-genocide days -- but The Sympathizer offers hope that the mental wells of writers haven't yet run dry. 
 Very highly recommended, one of my few favorite novels of the year. Read it slowly. Take your time with it. Savor it. It's that kind of book.

 To say the least, this book was amazing in every was possible. Leigh Bardugo is able to make me laugh, cry, smile uncontrollably, and cry some more all in the course of only a few pages. How does she do it? I have no clue. My obsession with her books has just gone up times 100000 because of Crooked Kingdom. 
 There WILL be spoilers for Six of Crows but all Crooked kingdom spoilers WILL be hidden 
 Also, I've been saying for months that this book was going to destroy me emotionally, and I was so right. I think that just goes to prove my amazing psychic abilities. 
 How do I even begin describe this book? 
 I can't really say the plot summary of this without spoiling it too much, so bear with me here. A week after the events of Six of Crows, we start off with our amazing crew (minus a member) trying to figure out how to get the amazing Wraith, who is being held in captive by the not so amazing Jan Van Eck, back. It's full of twists and turns and yet another daring, impossible heist mission with a bit of romance sprinkled in here and there. We're also reunited with our lovable cast of criminals and thieves that you can't help but love with every ounce of your heart. 
 Inej is still my favorite. I love her so so so much. She's broken on the inside, but incredibly strong and powerful. As said in the musical Hamilton, she's definitely does not throw away her shot. Inej is so small she can blend into the shadows and sneak around Ketterdam, following people for blocks without getting noticed, earning her the nickname "the Wraith". 
 "My mother is Ketterdam. She birthed me in the harbor. And my father is profit. I honor him daily." 
 Kaz is even more amazing in this book than in the first (who could've thought that possible???). He continues to surprise everyone with the tricks and schemes up his sleeves. He's even darker in this book too, with all his threats and bluffs that leave you thinking "this guy is actually insane" until you realize that he was making it up and then you just want to reach across the page and give him a huge hug, because how could you not? I love Kaz so much, and his background still breaks my heart into a million tiny little pieces.  That scene at the end with him and Inej holding hands melted my heart. I will never stop shipping these two. And they've both been some really crappy stuff that's kind of stopped them from having these relationships. I mean Inej was sold into slavery at the Menagerie and all that stuff with Kaz and his brother? I can totally see why those two kind of had a hard time sorting through their feelings. And in the end, you know what? They hold hands. I don't think I've ever been happier about two characters just holding hands.  
 I love Nina in this book so much! She's so strong and powerful (literally...), and she goes through so much in this book. Her background isn't as bad as some of the other character's (trust me, it's still bad), but wow, does she go through some really bad and heartbreaking stuff in this book. All the while though, she continues to surprise people with the strength after all she's endured. Nina may not seem deadly, but wow, she is. I love her so much. 
 ...but for the first time since he'd looked into Nina's eyes and seen his own humanity reflected back at him, the war inside him quieted. 
 We'll find a way to change their minds, she'd said, All of them, He would locate Nina. They would survive this night. They would free themselves of this damp, misbegotten city, and then... Well, then they'd change the world. 
 And Matthias! I've always loved him, but he's never been my favorite like Nina, Kaz, and Inej. Matthias is so amazing in this book though. I love him so much more than I ever thought I would. He's not as vicious and deadly as some of the other characters (take the other three above for example), but he still has his super deadly vicious moments. Plus, his romance with Nina is just the most adorable thing in the history of adorable things. Can you tell that I ship them uncontrollably?  THAT ENDING KILLED ME THOUGH. I NEVER REALIZED JUST HOW MUCH I LOVED HIM UNTIL IT WAS TOO LATE *cries eternally* AND POOR NINA, TOO  
 Jesper is nothing short of hilarious. Even in the worst of situations he's always there to make some kind of joke or sarcastic remark all the while being super deadly and amazing. If you met him on the street, you probably wouldn't believe that he is actually a member of a vicious gang and has killed before. I still can't believe it. He's super awkward too, which makes him even more adorable. I liked him a lot more in this book to be honest. 
 "You're stupid about a lot of things, Wylan, but you are not stupid. And if I ever hear you call yourself a moron again, I'm going to tell Matthias you tried to kiss Nina. With tongue." 
 Wylan wiped his nose on his sleeve. "He'll never believe it." 
 "Then I'll tell Nina you tried to kiss Matthias. With tongue." 
 And the award for best character growth goes to Wylan Van Eck. Seriously. Wylan is amazing in this book. Please don't kill me, but he was my least favorite in Six of Crows. I know, I know! I didn't get how everyone loved him so much, but now I totally do. Wylan has been through a lot and we learn all of it in this book from his POV. His father treated him terribly growing up, but Wylan still continues to be super kind and caring, but he also becomes much stronger and deadlier here. IT'S WONDERFUL!  Wylan and Jesper are so adorable together. That scene with Kuwei was hilarious, and then when Wylan was getting tailored, eeeek. I'm really happy these two got together, they're so cute.  
 The writing was A++++++++. Leigh Bardugo can make me feel a thousand emotions all at once with her witty dialogue and beautiful writing. AND THE PLOT TWISTS??? All those just come out of nowhere. I'm sitting there, reading my book, and all of a sudden I'm like "WHOA, what just happened? THAT WAS AMAZING!!!". Seriously though, Leigh Bardugo has such beautiful writing, which is hard to come across in a fantasy book as action packed as this. Her use of metaphors and detail are wonderful. 
 Crows remember human faces. They remember the people who feed them, who are kind to them. And the people who wrong them too. They don't forget. They tell each other who to look after and who to watch out for." 
 We continue to learn even more about this amazing world! Like if you thought you learned enough in the first four Grisha books, you were wrong. We learn a lot about Ketterdam/Kerch here and we see how much the countries have developed since the war. Leigh Bardugo paints a perfect picture in your head of this world with her great worldbuilding and gorgeous writing. 
 Let's see, what else? 
 Well, the heist in this book was wonderful as well. So unlike the one in Six of Crows, but still amazing, with lots of little ones mixed in. And there are so many twists and turns you don't even know. The whole plot was just so wonderful, and still very different than any other YA book I've ever read. I mean, where are all of our YA heist books full of deadly but lovable characters like these books?! 
 "Have any of you wondered what I did with all the cash Pekka Rollins gave us?" 
 "Guns?" asked Jesper. 
 "Ships?" queried Inej. 
 "Bombs?" suggested Wylan. 
 "Political bribes?" offered Nina. They all looked at Matthias. "This is where you tell us how awful we are," she whispered. 
  Okay, but I really need to discuss this book with those of you who have read it. 
 The whole Van Eck thing was really interesting. I didn't really grasp their whole plan at first, maybe because it wasn't fully described or I was just half out of it, but wow, that was amazing. One minute Ravka is bidding on Kuwei, and the next we find out that it's basically Van Eck's money. And then because of what Kaz was able to do, Van Eck was turned in for doing all these things and stealing money when really he didn't do it. He so deserved it though, and can I tell you how happy I am that he's now stuck in Hellgate? To be honest, I'm kind of glad none of the villains died, just another way this book was unlike so many. 
 The ending tore me into a million little pieces. So I read a spoiler about the death on here by complete accident, so I knew it was coming. That didn't make me any less emotional though. Like when reading Deathly Hallows, I knew about all the deaths but I still cried so hard. I felt so bad for Nina though, you don't even know. Her and Matthias were finally happily together, and then he dies. It was so unexpected to! As they said, everyone was supposed to make it out, but one didn't, and he wasn't even doing something that was part of their plan when he was killed, just all the more heartbreaking. 
 Oh and the scene when Kaz reunites Inej with her parents? *heart breaks even more* We didn't really get to see much other than Inej running up to them, but it still made me so happy. Inej had been hoping that maybe she would find her parents when she traveled to Ravka, but instead they're their in Ketterdam, and it's just so sweet! I think she really deserved that moment  
 Overall, I loved this book so much. It was beautiful. It made me cry and laugh and smile and want to scream all at once. If I could, I would rate it 100000000/5 stars because I loved it just that much.

4.5 stars -- I almost feel bad not giving this a full 5 stars, but I didn't enjoy the Ruth chapters as much so I'm going to hold back half a star. 
 WOW! This book is deeply emotional. I was on the verge of tears many times. Nao's story really touched me, and I would have loved this book even if the Ruth storyline was absent and it was just about Nao. Actually, it took me a long time to realize the character Ruth in the book was supposed to be the author. Of course I noticed the character shared the author's name, and my immediate reaction was that it was weird for the author to give the character both her own name and ancestry. It wasn't until halfway through the book that I discovered the characters Ruth and Oliver are actually the author and her husband. I learned this after deciding that I didn't like character-Ruth very much--she seemed so cold to her husband, and to their dear cat!--so then I felt conflicted: I disliked person/character-Ruth, yet I loved the story this same individual had created.) 
 I had so many feelings about this book, yet I don't know what to write here. Maybe I should give it 5 stars, not 4. Hmm... 
 I started reading the book on a plane, at a time when I felt extremely tired and was having trouble focusing. I thought there was no way I could read a book in that state of mind, but I figured I'd give the first few pages a shot. Well, they hooked me, completely and thoroughly. I plowed through half of the book despite feeling exhausted, so that says a lot about its quality and how much I enjoyed it. I had a hard time putting it down--I had to know what happened to Nao next! Again, I wasn't very invested in the Ruth chapters (I liked how Ruth's actions affected Nao's life, but I disliked the rambling about Schroedinger's cat and parallel universes at the end of the novel. ), but I adored Nao and cared deeply about her. She made me feel all sorts of things, and for me personally, I love any book that evokes emotions in me.

I can't really say anything good about this book, except that the writing itself was well done. But the plot was meaningless, the characters pointless, and about halfway in, I realized that I. Could. Not. Do. It. I could not finish this book. So I skimmed the rest, and read the last couple of chapters to see how it ended. 
 Why is it that Rowling, who can create the most deep, emotional characters in her Harry Potter series managed to write an adult book that is completely without a soul? Is it just that she's trying too hard to distance herself from her previous works?

I really liked this one, and would have liked it more if it wasn't only the first 1/3 of the story (but that's a rant I've gone into many times so won't here). 
 Kelsea is a typical protagonist from a typical fantasy novel*- hidden away in the forest until she's 19, she is now of age to claim her throne from her evil uncle. Assassination attempts and righteous indignation at the state of her subjects abound, and Kelsea is a likeable heroine. Her personal guard is also made up of good men, and there is a dashing outlaw to provide some romantic tension (not in this book, really, but I'm sure it will come up later). A quick, compelling read, and I will be watching for the next installment in her story. 
 *the setting is, at first glance, very typical for fantasy novels- basically medieval, with everyone riding horses or driving carts, lots of sylvan forest and towering castles. BUT. There are tantalizing hints that the setting is not what we think it is, and seems rather to be taking place either sometime in the future of our world, or maybe in an alternate reality from ours (references are made to the Americans, the capital city is New London, and there's mention of The Hobbit and LOTR and "the seven volumes of Rowling", among other hints). I really think it's wanting to find out exactly what's going on here that is intriguing me enough to want to keep reading, although I really do like Kelsea.

Dru Anderson has been raised in an unconventional fashion. Her father is a hunter of the supernatural and she has been trailing after him for years. Then one night her father doesn't come back from a hunt alive but as a zombie. Dru spends the rest of the book in a disbelieving haze, trying to come to terms with his death and her current situation. 
 She befriends goth loner Graves and together they attempt to make sense of what has happened to Dru. Dru is a sarcasm-loving ass kicker and Graves is sharp and witty. Together they embody the time honored combination of hilarity and true friendship. 
 Why do I love this book so much? It's not just one thing--it's the entire package. Sarcastic ass kicker who tends to lapse into tears. Best friend who is more than he seems. Strange vampire who smells like apple pie. What isn't there to love? St Crow leaves us with more questions than answers in this book. You'll have to read the rest of the series to figure it all out but it's certainly worth a read. It's your typical YA novel with a bit of twist so it's not entirely generic. Give it a try--you won't regret it.

My cousin Rachel is a devilishly interesting book written by Daphne du Maurier. This book begins with the narrator Philip Ashley regretting his behaviour to Rachel. What has happened? Who is this Rachel? What follows, in the remainder of the book, is one of the most well fleshed out stories ever written. 
 It is a character study of how one's feelings to another person, colours or distorts their behaviour in one's eyes. What, yesterday felt completely innocuous, today attains a completely sinister purpose. It is in these questions that this book excels so well. 
 Before proceeding further, I would advise people who are reading the viargo ebook edition to skip the Sally Beauman introduction, as it gives some mild spoilers. While, reading this book, it is advisable to do so with an open mind. This is essential as the reader, depending on one's gender, inclinations etc like the characters in the novel, reaches different conclusions about each character. 
 The novels begins with a 23 year old man child called Philip Ashley, reminiscing about his cousin Ambrose. Ambrose, is a father figure to Philip, having raised him like his very own heir. Having become old and suffering from poor health, Ambrose visits Italy on the advice of doctors. There, he meets another cousin Rachel, who he subsequently marries, much to the consternation of Philip. Ambose, extends his stay in Italy and communicates with Philip by means of letters. These letters , initially full of familial bliss, slowly take on a morbid tone. Ambrose suspects his wife of poisoning him. Reading this, Philip decides to visit him in Italy. however, he arrives too late and finds Ambrose dead and buried. What follows next, is a good psychological study on motivations and their colouring one's opinions of others. 
 I recommend this book to all literature and mystery fans.

i decided as an opening salvo for 2013 i'd commit to reading the 2500-page No Man's Land story arc and finally got my hands on this opening volume. the nice {?} thing about a disaster story is that the artists spend a lot of ink doing splash pages of things blowing up and falling down, so this was a page-turner in that sense. overall i enjoyed most of it, but will break it down here into the good, bad, and ugly. 
 good: compelling story-telling that's not about people in tights for the most part. superheroes who have to deal with something we can recognize as reality for a change. some genuinely interesting tension between bats and huntress over what to do with looters, etc. a surprisingly strong story about blackgate prison in which bats barely appears. nice character work with babs/oracle and gordon and even bullock (though i dislike him). 
 bad: very dated comic book writing (not as bad as Death in the Family, say, but definitely a product of its time. incredibly inconsistent artwork (and some of it very bizarre/poor) ~ this is especially unfortunate given the epic sweep of the story. it's hard to relate to the horror of gotham in ashes when it just looks like an inky scribble. a weak story about arkham during the earthquake was also very silly and disappointing. 
 ugly: some of the tie-ins (azrael, yes, but catwoman especially) are badly drawn, stupidly written, and not very well integrated into the whole (a poison ivy/catwoman episode was just flip flip flip for me). also, there's this boring character named spoiler who just needs to go away (though i am sure she won't). 
 i did not expect to read through this first volume so fast. some other critics have lambasted this for the villain called "quakemaster", but i actually think he was very well done (bats thinks he's full of it from the onset, so why should the readers take him seriously?). he was a nice way of integrating a "super-villain" into story in which a natural disaster is what's actually center-stage. 
 despite the inconsistency of the art and writing, this is an impressive project that appears very well-coordinated so far when you think about the number of comics through which it originally ran. if the successive volumes are at least as good as this, i won't feel like my time was poorly spent.

 This book surprised the hell out of me. 
 It's been on my TBR list for quite some time, and I happened to come across it when it was free. I grabbed it up and figured I'd read it eventually. I read the blurb to refresh my memory, and then I read the first couple of pages just to get an idea of the quality of the writing. 
 I never put it back down. 
 It didn't matter that it was hot-as-balls out and that the ocean water was calling my name. It didn't matter that my family came back and told me about the cool fish they saw. I was absorbed into this world of Liliana's and Ryan's, and so I sat and I read and read and read until it was over and I was wishing for more. 
 I loved the fact that the main character was Spanish and a young mother. A lot of the times the MC is blonde and single and young and it's hard to relate to someone like that when I am, in fact, Spanish and a young mother. A lot of the things her mother said to her sounded like something my own would say to me. 
 Lilian's character was strong and sure. She did everything in her power to make her mother and Javier happy, even if it meant putting aside her own desires for a life. The relationship between her and her son brought tears to my eyes more than once. I couldn't even imagine having to deal with all of the things she was going through. I admired and respected her, which in turn made me hope for her. 
 Ryan- god did I feel for him. The author did such a good job of portraying his emotions without lessening his masculinity. Everything about him was broken, but not ugly. He was a perfect balance of dark and light. 
 I love the part that Alex, Ryan's cousin, played in their relationship. He cared for Lili enough to stay away from her but he cared for Ryan enough to push him towards her. I will definitely be reading his book when it comes out. 
 The plot, even though common, was unique because of the writing. There were few grammatical errors, easily overlooked. It was angsty and dramatic, but never over the top. The whole I-want-you-but-I-shouldn't thing could have been annoying, as it usually is, but I was seriously invested in these characters and rather enjoyed their internal struggles. 
 This was a solid 4 stars for me.

I read Cat Winter's debut novel, In the Shadow of Blackbirds, last year and I immediately fell in love. The stunning combination of the 20th century setting, the historical photographs and a moody love story blew me away. In many ways The Cure for Dreaming is very different: but it's yet again an amazing book. 
 Set during the highdays of the Suffragist movement, The Cure for Dreaming tells to story of one girl trying to find her place in the world. Women are in an awkward position; they want agency and freedom, but there are many protesting voices that find that women belong inside of the home. Trying to cure Olivia from her "useless dreams" (namely going to college and having a carreer), Olivia's father hires a hypnotist, the young Henri Reverie. 
 Writing about feminist movements is tricky business. It's easy to alienate your reader if your story becomes too preachy or obvious. We all know that women have souls (something that sparked debate during the 19th century) and that they are equal to men. At least, we all should know this. Ms Winters did a great job at not making men in general seem like bad guys, a common problem in female rights centered books. The truth is that many men are feminist, and that many women aren't. The Cure for Dreaming displays this pretty well. 
 However, I don't think it was all perfect. At one point Olivia can see how the world really is. This means that she can see some kind of life energies. Some people are very dim (and unhappy) while others shine brightly (happy people). Women with their husbands are either described as normal looking or dim or even invisible. Suffragists, just girls hanging out, are all considered super bright. I would think this is an overstatement; just because you're free doesn't mean you're happy, and just because you have a husband doesn't make you oppressed. It's a minor detail that didn't stop me from enjoying the story, but it did make me think about how reality is much more complicated than that. 
 The Cure for Dreaming is a historical novel with a paranormal tinge, depending on whether you believe hypnosis is really possible beyond a certain extend. The fact that Olivia sees the true nature of people, they often appear to her like vampires or other terrible monsters. This gives the book a flair of horror and a nightmareske aspect, although it never descends into something truly scary. 
 The major conflict in the book is the one between Olivia and her father. Her father thinks he is doing the right thing by caging Olivia, making her into a submissive housewife so she can marry a good match. However, his motives are also selfish, because he wants Olivia to stay close and not turn into her mother. This ambivalence was well done, and her father was a very interesting character for me. 
 There is a small romantic plotline in the book, which isn't the focus of the story. It was a very nice one though, very realistic and dependant on small moments, instead of the epic love storiea Hollywood seems to favor. I was especially thrilled over how the romance was resolved. It was done perfectly in the spirit of the book and fitted wonderfully. 
 The Cure for Dreaming is a really good and interesting book, and Winters' talent for worldbuilding shines yet again. It's a slightly less moody and creepy sister to In the Shadow of Blackbirds, but with just as strong a story.

I'm not sure I could ask for a better book to review on Valentine's Day. Dash and Lily's blossoming romance is one of the sweetest, funniest and most honest that I've read. 
 I loved the concept of this story, that the couple meet through a diary, performing a set of tasks and clues before they ever see each other face to face. The book opens with Dash's point of view as he finds the little diary stashed in-between his favourite author's works in a bookshop. The book dares him to prove himself by following some clues, eliminating anyone who the diarist would not be romantically interested in. Dash passes the test, but instead of leaving his name and number with the specified shop assistant, he leaves the diary, with a new set of clues. And so the dairy-flirting-treasure-hunt begins. 
 Through the opening chapter, both Dash and the reader gain a sense of what kind of person Lily is, and both are completely wrong! In the very next chapter the reader is introduced to the real Lily, a shy, optimistic and naive girl whose brother placed the diary in the bookshop in the hopes of finding her a date. As the story progresses, it becomes clear that not only are Lily and Dash almost exact opposites, they are also each forming entirely the wrong impression of the other. Dash is snarky, sarcastic and suspicious, and he hates Christmas. Lily is open, optimistic and cheery, and she loves everything about this time of year. Dash thinks Lily's messages are ironic and her Christmas-themed clues are designed to tease him. Lily has a slightly more truthful impression of Dash (largely thanks to her helpful and hilarious relatives), but his sarcasm can sometimes fly over her head and she believes Christmas is all that's needed to cheer him up. 
 At first the situation seems hopeless, but then both Dash and Lily begin to change. Lily is right; Dash is, underneath the snark, a boy who needs a little more cheer and optimism in his life. Through Lily's kindness and joy (and some very good cookies), he does begin to open up a bit more and to look at the world in a better light. For the first time he begins to enjoy Christmas. And Lily needs her boundaries to be pushed a little, to be treated more like an adult and asked the important questions that only Dash seems willing to ask her. Lily is upset about many little things in her life, mostly all due to the over-protectiveness of her family - which, as she puts it, is what causes 'Shrilly' to emerge. Dash helps Lily to gain confidence in herself and to stick up for herself a little more. As Lily toughens a little, Dash softens a little; it is clear that they are actually perfect for each other after all. 
 The book is written very well, with a lot of heart but also a lot of humour. There were several laugh-out-loud moments, especially Dash's encounter with the local vigilante mummy-patrol. The characterisation is brilliant and it's this that really makes the book so fantastic. Both Dash and Lily are wonderful characters, and their relationship as well as their interaction with others is always realistic and enjoyable. For me, Lily was the stand out character - she was always truthfully written and the most sympathetic, and the one who changed the most throughout the story. There's also a fantastic range of side-characters who add plenty of humour and trouble to the plot. 
 Romantic, moving, funny and honest, and packed with great characters, Dash and Lily's Book of Dares is a wonderful story.

If you want to spend time with perhaps the greatest drama queens in literary history, then embrace this book. Any possible psychological depth is drowned under the over-the-top rhetoric and outrageously high-pitched melodrama generated by its main characters. Some of that excess almost makes the book trashily engrossing, but the exaggeration is so great it's hard to take seriously or be moved by. 
 Whether it was attempting to be the ultimate expression of dark, complicated romantic love or a harsh criticism of the destructive obsessiveness of the same, the book is saved from collapsing into pure farce only by the strength of Bronte's writing. But even that is tarnished by her device of having the story told through multiple viewpoints - each of which irritatingly has the same style and voice - the voice of Emily Bronte. I could not make it past two thirds of this.

 The underlying story is fun and clever: Emma believes herself to be so intuitive and perceptive about other people and their relationships, while the reader is seeing that she doesn't have any of it quite right. Some people she sees as cold are actually very nice, those she sees as clever also have a darker side, those she sees as silly or stupid can actually be quite perceptive and kind. She helps along one relationship (the Westons) and sees herself as a consummate matchmaker - unfortunately she steers one friend away from the man who will eventually be her husband, encourages this friend to fall for a man who is actually in "love" with Emma and ends up marrying someone else once rejected, Emma thinks she loves one man and then (when she realizes she doesn't) again tries to match her friend up with him, and she completely misses the surprise relationship of the book. Seeing her miss the boat and yet somehow not doubt her matchmaking prowess was really entertaining. 
 It's always a little dicey to read about women in classic literature - they (and particularly the supporting cast) are often portrayed as silly, vain, petty, jealous and with an appalling lack of curiosity OR as saintly women with incredible grace, charm, patience and tolerance. The main character often has some mix of good and bad qualities and experiences growth through the book - Emma is generally a good person who sometimes gets caught up by her own jealousy or sense of superiority or self-confidence. She does grow into a more understanding and self-aware person by the end of the book, which was gratifying to see. 
 One of the nice things about the book, especially for a summer read, is that everyone ends up where they should be. It's nice to have a happy ending, especially during the summer! I normally start out thinking that a book will rate a 3/5 and adjust from there; since this was Austen, I started out with about a 2! In the end, I give the book a 3.5/5, so it really was much better than I thought, but it's still not my favorite. 
 I will read more Austen (Pride and Prejudice is on my list for this year) and hope for the best. I don't think I will ever really be a fan, but I enjoyed the writing and just need to read her books when I'm in the right mood, which is true of most books!

 Remembrance and forgetting guide the multilayered narratives of Tan Twan Eng's luminous, Booker Prize nominated The Garden of Evening Mists. So important are they that they're personified as statues of twin goddesses within the titular Japanese-style garden that is found high in the mountains of Malaya. Teoh Yun Ling, a senior judge retiring from the Malaysian bench, is caught between different periods of her life, of remembering and forgetting. 
 Yun Ling has kept the reason for her retirement, and her subsequent return to the Cameron Highlands, secret from all but a few people: she has been diagnosed with aphasia, which means she will slowly lose her memories and her ability to process the meaning of words at all. Terrified but determined, she flees to the tea estate that once belonged to Aritomo Nakamura, a Japanese expatriate fabled for being the disgraced gardener of the Japanese emperor. This is not the first time she has made this journey. When she was 19, she and her sister Yung Hong were captured by the Japanese. The more attractive Yung Hong was pressed into service as a "comfort girl" for the soldiers. Ironically, her only escape came in the form of daydreams about Japanese gardens, an art form she fell in love with when the family visited Japan years earlier. 
 Yung Ling makes it out alive, but her sister does not, and she tries to cleanse her memory and her survivor's guilt by using her law degree to go after war criminals. Later, at the time of the Malayan Emergency, she goes in search of the emperor's gardener. Though she hates the Japanese for everything done to her, her sister, and her country, she seeks to heal her trauma and commemorate her sister by hiring Aritomo to create the garden of Yung Hong's fantasies. He refuses, instead offering a compromise: he will take Yung Ling on as an apprentice so that she can make the garden herself. 
 Now retired, Yun Ling relates these two periods of her life in her memoirs, and in her discussions with another Japanese professional: Professor Yoshikawa Tatsuji, who is interested in Aritomo's other artistic pursuits, namely ukiyo-e (wood-block prints) and horimono (masterful full-body tattoos). As she tells of the dire political state of Malaya in the 1950s, her work in the garden, her studies in Zen archery, and her unfolding love affair with Aritomo, she underscores it all with the horrors she endured and of the acts she participated in afterward in the name of vengeance. She begins to revisit stories and memories she has long worked to forget, and she finds herself drawing new lines of connection that unearth surprising mysteries and consequences. 
 Art, tea, guerilla warfare, politics, colonialism. Archery, tattooing, gardening, torture. Families torn apart, freedoms won and lost. . . so much happens across the decades of this quietly epic book. Tan evokes times, places, and pieces of history I had absolutely no idea about or understanding of and makes them come to life. Even as Yung Ling tries to hide her scars, physical and mental, after the war, she sees echoes of them in Magnus, her host, who was taken by the British during the Boer War and still harbours deep resentment and pain. As she remembers the pain she and her sister endured, she also remembers the war criminals she helped put to death. Layers of history and sorrow, of remembering and forgetting, come together to form an exquisitely sad work of art. 
 The writing in this book is just beautiful, wrapping the reader in the lush, misty green serenity of the Cameron Highlands while offering on a platter the atrocities humans are capable of. "Memory is like patches of sunlight in an overcast valley, shifting with the movement of the clouds," Yung Ling observes as she casts her eye back over her life. "Now and then the light will fall on a particular point in time, illuminating it for a moment before the wind seals up the gap, and the world is in shadows again" (p. 294). Tan jumps effortlessly between the three major time periods of the tale, employing past and present tense to differentiate, and creating distinct voices for Yung Ling, now bitter and filled with hatred, now serene but filled with sadness. The juxtaposition of opposites throughout the novel works in a similar way: the city of Kuala Lumpur versus the country of the Cameron Highlands; colonial versus national interests; heated rainforests versus cool mountains. Remembrance versus forgetting. 
 Aritomo is a fascinating character, full of surprising angles and well-drawn flaws and strengths. His absence is as important in the "present" narrative as his presence is in the past. The art professor Yoshikawa apologizes to Yun Ling for what his people did to her all those years ago, and she dismisses the apology as meaningless. What she appreciates most about her time with Aritomo is that he never once asked for forgiveness of his people. Instead, he showed her his humanity through his actions and his lessons, and through the intuitive love that springs between them. 
 A major lesson Aritomo teaches Yun Ling in the art of Japanese gardening is that of shakkei, or borrowed scenery, "taking elements and views from outside a garden and making them integral to his creation" (p. 25). From the reflection of the sky in a pond to a mountain in the distance framed in the garden by vines, shakkei also takes on a deeper meaning: Yung Ling suggests that the exiled Aritomo's memories of his life in Japan are a form of borrowed scenery, brought into his Japanese-style garden in the mountains of Malaya but never truly enough to bring him back to Japan. The same might be said of Yung Ling's memories: the ways in which she must order them in the present, the ways her suppression of them have ordered her life up until this point. 
 I read The Garden of Evening Mists on vacation, and as I sat on the sun-drenched, postcard-perfect beach, I wept openly during the final chapter. This book of tragedy and healing, trauma and forgiveness, and forgetting and remembrance, is exquisite. It is, perhaps, my favourite book of 2012, and I urge you to pick up a copy.

Cassandra Clare has given me another book to love. It's love, but it's a different love than the previous 3 books. 
 Unfortunately, in this book, I liked Jace just a tid bit less. I'm not sure why, but I'm assuming because it's about him not being able to express his true love for Clary, which isn't really his fault. So I guess I'm just mad at Cassandra Clare. I understand she must make her characters go through so many things to help them grow, but really, this is getting to be A LOT of unfortunate events to the same characters over and over. I wish it was mixed up a little. 
 Clary and Jace's struggles are nothing less than exciting though. The tension between them is so high and it leads to some very passionate events, which no one is complaining about! 
 I like the fact that she introduced new characters into the mix at well. There are references and even a character from the Infernal Devices series in the plot now. I love Kyle's character and I really like who he ends up getting along with. I even find it very humorous! 
 Since there are new characters, she had to cut back on some other characters face time. I'm really happy that even though she didn't have the characters as involved, she made their relationships grow, a lot. This book is basically a HUGE leap in the relationship department for just about every single character. Everyone is having relationship issues/problems. Seriously, everyone. But I'm not complaining. Makes it fun of course! 
 SPOILER ALERT---- Seriously, big one so quit reading here if you've not finished. Like all the way finished, because it's about the last 4 pages I'm talking about. 
 Cassandra had to keep the suspense up and the plot going I understand. The ending left me sad, mad and astonished but more than anything, it left me heart-broken. Jace has been through so much, I just can't believe he's going through even more now. The only thing that bothers me about the way Jace acts is the way Clary perceives or handles it. She knows somethings up and yet she barely decides to do anything about it throughout the book in person. When she doesn't see him she makes an effort, but if the person I loved was acting weird and cold, I probably wouldn't let up until I figured out what was wrong with them. She did a good job at the end though of making him talk to her. I give her that. I think I just wish someone else besides Jace (or especially SImon) would get picked on. Those poor boys. Seriously, I'm not sure how they are even living anymore. 
 I think what really bothers me is that there is no truly happy in this book, until the very end maybe before the last 4 pages. Everyone is high-strung and horrible things are happening to everyone. It's like there's a depressing tone. And the fact that Jace and Clary's relationship has a huge black cloud over it, just made it harder to get through unconcerned. 
 It really amazes me how she tied so many things from the first three books into this book when she didn't even know she'd be writing it. The loopholes she left in the first three and completely addressed in here, and more are even added! 
 Overall, fabulous book and that rediculous cliff-hanger will leave me anxiously awaiting COLS for a whole year. This wait is going to be tough.

The reason that I read Graceling was because it was included in The Noob's Guide to Fantasy Reads. And, that it what I am - a noob in the fantasy genre. Indeed, it takes a while getting into fantasy books, and this one is no different. 
 Graceling was a pretty good book, in my opinion. It has a good plot, I love the main characters, and the writing style was good. But the thing is, I felt like it lacked the element of excitement, when I would just turn the page until I got to the last one, pause for a while and process what just happened. With this book, I'm liking it, but I wouldn't mind putting down the book to do other things, and I wouldn't be mad if I was interrupted. Which is why it took me so long to finish the book. However, I still really enjoyed this one. 
 The strong heroine that I always enjoy is present in this book. Katsa definitely is a strong woman, and not just physically. She can stand on her own two feet and doesn't like relying on anyone. She has a pretty great character development in this novel. She started from being enslaved by King Randa, to setting out on her own. From acting on her temper, to learning how to control it. From never letting feelings get to her, to letting go and accepting her feelings. 
 I didn't really like Po in this novel. He always keeps things hidden from anyone, even Katsa, letting others figure things out before he confesses. Sometimes I'm really annoyed at him and I want to beat him up like Katsa wanted to, except I wouldn't know how to and Katsa would. 
 My favorite character from this novel is Bitterblue. She's just 10 years old, but she understands so much. She's a princess, but she's no brat. She's usually quiet, but when help is needed, no one needs to tell her to do so. She's very helpful, strong, understanding, and wise beyond her years. 
 Overall, this was a pretty good book, but it lacks excitement.

 Lilah returns to her home town for the last semester of her senior year in high school. She left two years ago after a tragic event and she hasn't returned so far. When she arrives home, her father lets her know that her childhood best friend, Chase Matthews is also moving into their house because of his drunken father. Chase and Lilah always had a special bond since they were born, but they didn't speak with each other since Lilah moved to Austen to her Aunt two years ago. 
 Lilah is so lost, in so much pain and grief and hunted by the past of the mistakes of others. She is no longer the popular smiling blond girl from the dance team, she has now a black pixie haircut, with sadness in her eyes and she tries to keep everyone at arm's length from her, but Chase is determined to trying breaking through her walls and to find his Lilah again. He tries to help her find her way out from the darkness but it's not an easy journey. She has to let off so much remorse and so much pain.

As the story flicks back and forth between present and past, threads of the story slowly reveal and step by step the whole picture starts to fit together. The way this story unfolds is flawless and the writing style is also astonishing. 
 The book was emotional and was dealing with some serious issues. Before the release, the author drew attention to the fact that maybe not everybody will love this story. Yes, this story is raw and emotional but guys, I have to tell you that this book has so much deepness and beauty! I loved every single line of this book! I loved all the roughness around the edges, all the imperfections of the characters and I really am glad that she decided to publish this book, despite the first rejection of a publisher because I felt that she poured her heart into every page.

 Emma by Jane Austen Review: 
 I'm going to be completely honest. I actually really liked this book, contrary to the opinions of some people. I liked this book, even though I've had many mixed/negative feelings and opinions about the characters and events that are in this novel, all in all I really enjoyed this book. This book made me feel so many emotions. I laughed, I screamed, I smiled, I gasped, I was pissed, I was caught off guard, I was shock and surprised, I was annoyed, I was angry, and I was feeling so many things while reading this book. You see that's what I really like when I read a book. When it makes me feel these raw emotions and a variety of feelings, not only anger, sadness, or just happiness. This novel felt so crazy in my opinion. It took me up and down and all around, like a roller coaster. But in reality, this book is so mellow, well in comparison to the novels that I usually read. The YA novels I read are so action-packed: Dystopian, sci-fi, fantasy, mystery, etc. You know? Something exciting would be happening in every chapter, like exploding buildings, death, fighting and that sort of stuff. But the difference that I really enjoyed was that usually YA dystopian (and others) novels are usually packed with a lot of world building. The authors often build these worlds and write about these backgrounds, plot development, and information, and often miss out on a lot of character development. But this novel is realistic fiction. It was contemporary when first published and there was no need for world building and I think that was very interesting. It was all about the characters, the character development, the characters' interactions, their dialogue, and I think this way I was more rapt in the characters and more connected to them, leaving me engrossed in the book. 
 I've always wanted to read a Jane Austen novel, but I never found the time because all of these YA novels were calling out at me. So when there was an option to read a Jane Austen novel for my English class, I jumped at the chance. I needed that push, but I always pictured myself reading Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice or Sense and Sensibility first. However, I'm really happy that I read Emma. This story is about a wealthy, intelligent, beautiful, and slightly spoiled big headed young lady named Emma Woodhouse and she has this hobby. Match making. She tries to set up her new friend, Harriet Smith, with the local vicar, Philip Elton AKA Mr. Elton. The book takes a turn and there are many surprises and witty banter and enjoyable scenes. I really enjoyed this book, and though some people may be disgusted or repulsed by reading about these "wealthy stuck up snobs" but I don't mind reading stuff like that, in fact this book isn't really like that, but I can understand how they might perceive it. Anyways, this book starts out really annoying, especially in volume 1. 
 I think that Jane Austen did a really good job at making these characters... annoying. While reading the book (but not quite done), I had these very strong, severely enforced opinions about these characters, more specifically, why I hated them. However, nearing the end, my awful opinions got mixed up and muddled with all the revelations and the truth. Let's talk about the protagonist herself, Emma. She severely irritated me during Volume 1, but she was tolerable unlike other characters. My opinion about her is that she's this very young, intelligent, rich lady who takes pride in manners. She came off as a feminist to me, I don't know if anyone else saw her like that but whatever. She strong-headed, or in other words, she's stubborn. She cares a lot about social statuses. Grace, poise, and etiquette are things she takes very seriously. The reason why I found her so irritating was because she gave off this impression that she was very intelligent. But she was so oblivious to the fact that Mr. Elton was pining for her! I found that completely and utterly ridiculous! I mean I already knew that Mr. Elton was after her instead of Harriet prior to reading the book, and maybe that's why I found all the clues so obvious, but I think that even without prior knowledge, it was blatantly expressed. I know that there was character development in Emma, and that she's become wiser. However it's very muddled to me. What I mean is I can't pinpoint an exact location of growth or development. Anyways, my opinions about Emma aren't clear and very mixed. 
 I found Harriet extremely annoying! At first, I felt that Emma was just being mean when she was talking about how Harriet was so gullible and docile, but as the story progresses, I realized that Harriet was so... weak! She was spineless and submissive. I couldn't stand her. There was this one page were she agreed with everything Emma said and I could imagine her nodding/shaking her head crazily with big eyes looking up at Emma. I just couldn't... Then when it is revealed that Mr. Elton didn't want her, she was so irritating. She kept putting Mr. Elton on such a high pedestal and degrading herself! She was still obsessively infatuated with him, and she's that type of girl that would let a guy lower her self-esteem. I don't blame her though. I was like that and I was annoying too so yeah. Harriet is so frail and docile especially compared to Emma. Then we have this idea that Harriet has now fallen in love with Mr. Frank Churchill after being saved from gypsies, which I was a bit dubious about. I mean I never felt that Harriet had any affection towards him, but I NEVER suspected her to be in love with Mr. Knightley. "Harriet!" cried Emma, collecting herself resolutely-"Let us understand each other now, without the possibility of farther mistake. Are you speaking of-Mr. Knightley?" When I read his name, I literally dropped my iPad. I gasped so loudly! Then I screamed... Yeah and it was like two in the morning. In retrospect I should've seen it coming. Harriet is the type of girl to fall for a guy like Mr. Knightley especially after he offered to dance with her at that dance after Mr. Elton snubbed her. However the thing that really got me pissed off at her is when she got all big-headed at the end. "But now I seem to feel that I may deserve him; and that if he does choose me, it will not be anything so very wonderful." I got really irritated by her in the end. I think I liked her more when she had low self-esteem. In the end, however, I found this respect for her and an understanding. When her secret is revealed, I had to admit; I liked her a lot more, but not because of her new found wealth and status. I liked how she ended up pure and untainted by that social circle and their prejudice and ultimately ended up marrying a man who loved her for her and not her wealth or social status or popularity. I think that was brilliant and I admire her for that. 
 I never saw what was so appeasing and infatuating about Mr. Frank Churchill, no offense. I imagined him as this awkward, weird fellow who always smiled at Emma like a pedophile. I imagined him moving very jerkily and talking very unusual, and it has nothing to do with Jane Austen's writing style or the vernacular. I didn't like him to say the least. The revelation of his secret engagement with Miss Jane Fairfax made my hatred grow even more. He was lying, flirting with Emma, deceiving everyone, betraying everyone and being so queer at the same flipping time! I was so enraged. My notes say, "WHAT! I CANT BREATH! IS THAT WHY JANE WANTED NO KINDNESS FROM EMMA? BECAUSE FRANK TOLD HER ABOUT EMMA THINKING THAT SHE HAD AN AFFAIR WITH MR. DIXON!? HAVE THEY JUST BEEN TELLING EACH OTHER EVERY PRIVATE WORD TOLD TO THEM AND JUDGING EVERYONE??? WHAT THE FLIPPING FUCK! WHAT SORT OF ESPIONAGE IS THIS! I HATE THEM." I started freaking out and questioning his integrity and Jane Fairfax's pride. Why was she just sitting there watching her betrothed flirt with Emma like he hasn't a care in the world? Yeah, it was later revealed that this is the reason why she wanted no kindness from Emma so I guess it kind of explains it. My feelings totally changed, however, when we get to read the letter Frank wrote after the cats out of the bag. I found an understanding with him and his motives. I don't hate him anymore, but I don't love him and frankly I never did. 
 The only character that never annoyed, not once, was Mr. Knightley. I loooveeee Mr. Knightley. He is just so gentleman-like and chivalrous. He's intelligent, wise, and seemingly perfect. However, he does display anger, jealous, and resentment. I really liked how he did. I think it made him a more of a well-rounded and well developed person and character, which made me love him even more. Can I just say this one thing? I predicted that they would be together, mostly because I thought that Mr. Knightley was the man who Emma was going to set up with Harriet in the beginning. So I thought they were flirtatiously teasing each other in the very beginning of the book. Ha, little did I know back then... Even though, it was later revealed that Mr. Elton is the one Emma wants to match with Harriet, it was obvious that Mr. Knightley was a very significant character and I really loved him. I can't tell you that enough. He was witty and funny and so amazing. I fangirled so hard and shipped Emma and Mr. Knightley, even though he's like 37and Emma's like 20 and they're like 17 years apart... Nevertheless! I loved them together! 
 There were minor characters that got on my nerves as well, like Miss Bates (She could not SHUT UP), Mrs. Elton, and Mr. Elton, but in the end I could tolerate them. Anyway, I really didn't expect to enjoy this book as much as I did, and I would so recommend anyone to read it. It was amazing and I'm so glad this was the first Jane Austen novel I read. I can't wait to read another! 4 out of 5 stars! I really liked how everything ended up. The only reason I took about a star was because in the beginning, I wasn't very into the book, and I felt like it was dragging on with the whole Mr. Elton thing. I also gave it four instead of five because though I ended being okay with all the annoying characters, they were still annoying at one point and a majority of them too. Read the book! Whoo!

This is book is not really what I was expecting, and unfortunately, that is not a good thing in this case. I skimmed a good chunk of this book, mostly in the middle. I will say that the last third was pretty interesting and I wish that that had been spread out through the whole story. 
 Where to start. 
 First of all, I have to say that the beginning of the book feels like we're being thrown into the middle of the story. Now, sometimes that does work, this is certainly not to say that being flung headlong into action is not at all a way for a book to ever start. It can work and I have read books that approach it the right way. 
 This is not one of those books. Unfortunately, this was the start of a trend, which was that for a good chunk of the book I felt as though we didn't know what the hell was going on, and the world building and plot weren't necessarily compelling enough to make up for that fact. 
 The book is structured in a way that we go from point of view to point of view, written in the third person. Now, I'm not a particularly big fan of this type of writing - in GoT, for example, I ended up quite often just reading one character's story all the way through because that happened to be the one I cared the most about. I know it's common in fantasy, especially high fantasy, but it has to be very compelling to work. This book doesn't quite get that across, instead the jumps are rather disjointed and it didn't lend itself to the flow of the book at all. 
 A lot of this would be something that I could deal with if the world building was compelling enough, but unfortunately I found this lacking as well. This is mostly towards the beginning of the book, but this is crucial, and were it not for the fact that I got this as an ARC through Netgalley, I might not have finished it at all. I have a feeling some readers out there will find it too much of a slog and the early reviews seem to back that up. 
 Basically, there are too many questions and not enough answers, or more importantly, not enough depth to make the reader curious enough to keep on going. I had so many questions. Where is this set? When is this set? What's the explanation behind the technology and the culture? What's the background behind Quin's family, besides the fact that she's a 'Seeker'? Where did they come from? Why? The answers to a lot of these do come, but they come very late in the book and that left me stewing in frustration for much of the read. 
 Now, even all of this would be forgivable by me if the characters were fascinating and made me care, but they didn't quite hit the mark here, either. I mean, I guess I cared about Quin, but not overly so, because she wasn't strong enough against the backdrop of the confusing background, the lack of world building, and the plot that wasn't quite clearly laid out enough for me. 
 So all of this ended up with the book being a rather 'meh' experience for me, which was why I am giving it two stars. I know that it's going to be made into a movie, so maybe they can more more of it and skim over the bits that made it feel like a chore rather than a joy to read. 
 Disclosure: I received a copy of this book for free through Netgalley in exchange for an honest review.

Who Watches the Watchmen? 
 Days after reading this graphic novel and debating my feelings about it, taking time aside to re-read passages to see if I clearly understood them, and I am still shocked at how much I love the Watchmen comics. 
 When I first starting reading the graphic novel, I was very apprehensive to like it. It had been recommended to me over and over again by other comic book lovers, but I just couldn't understand the appeal. On the other hand, many people despised the Zack Snyder directed film from 2009, some people said it was too confusing and dense, and when I looked at the 1980s art style, I even scoffed at it. I truly didn't understand how this graphic novel was said to be one of the very best and how it could actually be referenced and compared to some of my favorites like Sandman. 
 Let me tell you, my feelings have changed. Here's just a few things I loved about this book: 
 -This graphic novel is wonderfully subtle. If you read it too quickly and don't stop to ponder the dialogue, you're going to miss something, and the story isn't going to wait around to explain it to you (like most comic books tend to do). 
 -The characters are complicated and each of them has a purpose to belong in this Cold War setting. Not one character is specifically likable, but they all feel important and real. 
 -On that note, Rorschach has become one of my favorite comic book characters of all time. He is SO cleverly written in these comics. 
 -I actually got to liking the art style! Art is such an important aspect to me when reading comics, and the art style really wore on me, even if I wasn't a fan at first. 
 Overall, this can become one of my favorite graphic novels of all time, and this was very unexpected for me! 
 I don't think that this is a graphic novel for everyone (there's not a whole lot of superheroes-being-cool, but rather, this is a story of after superheroes-being-cool), but if you really enjoy superhero stories and want to explore topics of justice and morality and what makes a superhero, I would definitely recommend this one.

One of my biggest joys as a reader is to find a book that, regardless of its subject matter, enthralls me with its artistry. Gold Fame Citrus qualifies for that description. In a way, at least for me, the story line for a book like this almost doesn't matter, because its very existence is what does. 
 Claire Vaye Watkins limns a view of the desiccated afterworld of the American Southwest, when its water woes have become its no-water existence - and its characters and its biology and its non-religion and its near-future and its beauty and its slight hope. She does this with a style that varies widely, depending on the atmosphere and feelings she wants to elicit, and the variety works wonderfully. 
 The characters are vivid (even in the white-out conditions of drifting sand dunes), and the variety of approaches to examine their lives are rich and captivating. Luz, Ig, Ray, Jimmer, Levi, Dallas - I know you all, now. 
 And Claire, I know you too as a magnificent writer.

 Logan and Gwen's long awaited first date finally takes place but as expected, in true Frost fashion, it blows up spectacularly. Too bad that spilling coffee onto the Spartan's lap is the least of her problems. Gwen's first meeting with her beau's dad doesn't exactly go well either; overprotective parents are one thing but arresting your son's teenage girlfriend seems like overkill to me. Crimson Frost takes off running and doesn't let up until Reaper bodies litter the floor. Literally. This is another fabulously bloody installment in Jennifer Estep's Mythos Academy series! 
 After Gwen's arrest, things go from bad to worse for her and even grandma Frost's attempt to cheer her up with comfort food from the Pork Pitt falls short. My heart ached for our Gypsy girl because after three books, she was finally beginning to find her place at the academy and this novel felt like that for every step forward she took, she got knocked back by two. It was a little shocking how quickly Gwen's classmates and even a few teachers turned against her. Thank goodness for Logan, Daphne and Carson! Frost also gains a shadow in this installment in the form of a third year Mythos student named Alexei, who's a new addition to this series. At first this Protectorate wannabe rubbed me the wrong way but he gradually proves that he's more than just a yes-man and I have a feeling that he'll be tagging along with Gwen's crew in future books. 
 I like how you never really know who to suspect in these novels; Reapers can be anyone. So far they've been mostly students but in this installment, even the Protectorate's not above suspicion and they're supposed to the law enforcement of the Pantheon. I had a difficult time trusting any of them, including Linus, which added even more complications to Gwen and Logan's relationship. The back-and-forth smack talk between Vic and Lucretia is hilariously barbaric. These two are out for blood and aren't afraid to advertise that fact. I was also right there with Frost on this one; what the heck is up with the stone statues? Are they alive? Because they seemed kind of pissed off at Gwen over her supposed betrayal. I'm hoping that when they finally do come into play that it's spectacular because Estep has had me curious about them for quite some time now. 
 Poor Logan, that's all I'm really going to say on that front... This novel starts off on a high note where he's concerned but things quickly deteriorate from there; we all have a few "do not push buttons" and unfortunately his get bulldozed. However, he is a Spartan, the most dangerous and deadliest of all the warriors, and the best fighter at Mythos so I'm sure he'll come around in time. I just hope that it won't be too little too late. 
 Each Mythos Academy book has been bloodier than the last which makes Crimson Frost a very fitting title for this installment. This is definitely one of the better YA series' out there now bring on Midnight Frost!

The final book in the Razorland trilogy is completely and utterly satisfying. I didn't read the other two books in the series (Enclave and Outpost) until I got my hands on this ARC at ALA, so I read all 3 within a couple weeks of each other so everything was really fresh in my mind and I didn't have to wait and wait for the next book. As the books went on, each one was longer then the one before it, which I think is perfect since we need more development as we get to know the characters and the horrifying world Aguirre has created. 
 Characters: Deuce is perfection. She's one of those girls that you really want to succeed and is so brave you envy her, but at the same time you want to bang your head on the table when she doesn't express her feelings towards Fade, who is near perfection as a male lead. Sure he has his shortcomings, but the two of them together are utter book bliss and as much as you want Fade for yourself you definitely want him with Deuce. Also,(as I point out in all my other Y.A. reviews) their first love scene was also perfection for a young adult novel. Yay Aguirre!! Just enough description to know what they are doing, perfectly timed within the novel, and amazing tension and emotion between the two. This is how a love scene is done! (y.a. authors take note!)As for minor characters, I love them all so much and some of the deaths were hard to take (the tears!) they were in a war for humanity and it was completely realistic and gut-wrenchingly emotional. 
 Plot: The story line for this one was just a continuation of the other 2, which is what you want in a trilogy. No need to add weird side stories or add on an even bigger bad that is coming for them, but easing up to the ultimate fight that we all knew was coming. The twist, which I won't give away, was surprising and shocking, but fit within the overall concept of fighting this horde of mutants that wanted to wipe out humans. I definitely didn't see it coming, which is why I'm not a writer, but the ending while bittersweet, was also hopeful. Plus that epilogue!! Oh if only Suzanne Collins had pow-wowed with Aguirre when writing the one in Mockingjay, then we wouldn't have had that sad-sack of an ending. The epilogue for Horde is perfection (have I used that word too much, yet?) 
 I would recommend this book for lovers of Marie Lu's Legend, Bick's Ashes (but only the first book, cause don't get me started on the other two), and for anyone who just wants a great y.a. series that won't disappoint.

I've been punched in the gut with this one. 
 More than that, it feels like a story that will linger in the recesses of my thoughts, occasionally illumined by a turn of the earth. This is an exquisitely wrenching coming-of-age story. It is also by turns difficult and sweet and tangy and uncomfortable and comforting. The realism and the bald honesty of internal conflict inject a beauty that is matched in the illustration style, one which is capable of both fear and tenderness. The graphics even shift in tone and density according to scene, and it is only afterward that the reader might reflect how immersive the story experience was. 
 This may seem an odd assessment. Many will instead focus on the narrative of first love and wonder at the snapshot I present. I'm not dismissing that at all, merely putting the thread in the context of the greater story. The question of longing, of a hunger for more, is core, and the exploration of whether that might be found in faith, in relationship, or in vocation is ripe, especially when we consider whether those obsessions become by definition mutually exclusive. 
 I don't agree with all the ideology or conclusions, but I do understand and empathize with them. The fact that I am haunted by this story -- in both word and image -- despite my differences is a testimony to its power and complexity.

I debated between three and four stars for this one. I enjoyed the book, but you'll understand from my basic description below why I was a bit hesitant about liking this book. 
 Aislinn (pronounced Ash-lin) is a virginal Catholic school girl who sees fairies (and they aren't sweet or cute). She's being pursued romantically by her friend Seth, an older, experienced college student and Keenan, a ruthless fairy king with a retinue of fairy concubines. 
 Yes, I did frame this in the most basic, most uncomfortable way, but I wanted you to understand why this book made me a bit uncomfortable. 
 So now that I've got you on board, the reason I did give this book a four star review was that it was action packed, fun to read, and Aislinn turned out to be pretty darn kick-ass. She took the future she was being handed and said, "Um, no. I'll work this out for myself, thanks." 
 Seth's a good guy, and Melissa Marr helps you understand that Keenan's actions are really all about preserving his peoples' welfare (well, other than the concubines, which is obviously my word choice not Marr's). Keenan's got a real witch of a mother who's basically trying to destroy both the human and fairy world, so you can see how he's a bit on edge about things and why he desperately wants to claim his full power. Unfortunately, to do that he needs to claim his fairy queen, and Aislinn's looking like a pretty good bet. 
 So there's lots of conflict, and, just because I thought it was neat, I'll mention that Seth lives in two converted railroad cars, which, of course, being made of steel (which uses iron) is pretty much anathema to fairies. 
 Overall, it was a fun, quick-paced book, and the end allayed most of my concerns (although you do still have a virginal Catholic schoolgirl main character, I'd just like to point out.) 
 P.S. After taking some time away from this book and reading several other awesome books, I'm afraid I had to downgrade this from 4 to 3 stars. It just didn't stick with me, and, I'm afraid to say, when there are books like Shadow and Bone and Poison Study out there in the YA genre, this book just doesn't hold up by comparison. Sorry, book.

As a hearing impaired person with an adoration for the famous hero/heroine trope, I was really interested in this book. However, since the publication date has been pushed back multiple times (now 2016!), I finally broke down and read the first five Wattpad chapters. 
 I still think the concept is a great idea and I like what little I've seen of the characters so far, but the Wattpad chapters don't accurately portray what it's like to be deaf or hearing impaired. Setting aside whether or not deaf people can enjoy music (they can), the syntax of sign-language, and the odds of Ali being verbal if she's been deaf her entire life, a smart phone is one of the biggest assets a hearing impaired person can have in the modern age. Yes, Ali and Jace wouldn't be able to just call each other, but they can certainly FaceTime or text. Furthermore, there are all kinds of apps now are made to assist deaf people, like text to speech apps or apps that will allow a deaf person to call a hearing person with an interpreter as an intermediary. Hell, if I could afford it, I could buy blue-tooth enabled hearing aids that would allow my phone to sync right to my aid. So Ali being deaf is not a reason for her not to have a cell. 
 I'm not rating this because the Wattpad chapters were posted in 2011 and, yes, there have been technological advances since then. Also, because it's not actually the book! I'm hoping that the author will do an extensive edit and re-write because I'm nuts for the concept and I think it could really be special.
