3.5/5 
 This book is split up into two short stories, the first one being a little over 100 pages, and the second one being a little under 50 pages. Both of them deal with grief and loss of a loved one whose passings were unexpected. Banana Yoshimoto's writing style is beautiful and eloquent, however I found that there was something quite elusive about her prose. I found myself not really immersed in the story at times, particularly in the first story. I also enjoyed Yoshimoto's inclusion of a transgendered character, who was never used as the butt of jokes, but stood as the nurturing, wonderful human that she was. 
 With the first story, while I registered the sorrow of the main characters and the themes that came up, I just couldn't connect with the characters. I have never dealt with the loss of a relative who I have been very close to and I think because of that, I wasn't able to understand their sense of anguish. I do see the importance of being present for those who are dealing with depression, no matter how little you can contribute to helping them in finding joy again. This is something I can connect with as I have been through this in the last couple of months actually. You should be there for other people, but not at the expense of your own well being, particularly if you find their emotional state triggering for yourself. I ended up giving this story a 3/5 rating simply because I feel that it is a good story that is also very well written, but I think this is just a case of me reading the right story at the wrong time in my life. 
 The second story I enjoyed much more. I was really able to empathize with the character and I definitely felt more drawn to her narrative than with that of the previous story. There were subtle elements of magical realism as well, which I really liked. While the first story took me several days to read, I finished this story is one sitting and I liked the allusions it made in mental illness (depression) being similar to having a fever. The toughest parts are hell to pull through but once you make it out of that alive, slowly and surely you will find the joys of life again. This story did a really good job and showing the normality of depression and our coping methods, no matter how strange they may seem to those who have never gone through similar situations. It normalizes the actions of those who suffer in a very real and relatable and I really commend Yoshimoto for doing that. I ended up giving this story 4/5 rating. 
 I highly recommend this book for those who may be going through a rough patch in life, whether it be the loss of a loved one or simply feeling like you are falling into a black hole. I am glad this book came into my life and I will be sure to return to this later on in my life.

Probably closer to a 3.5. 
 Generally entertaining adventure fiction. You have Grimm, captain of the Predator (not actually in service to the Albion navy, but engaging in a certain amount of privateering), Gwen and Benedict (scions of a wealthy Albion family, both soldiers), Master Ferus and his apprentice Folly (slightly mad manipulators of etheric energy) and Bridget (newly enlisted in the guard) and her cat Rowl (good heavens, how furious he'd be to hear himself described in such terms!) who get caught up in the opening maneuvers as war breaks out between Albion and a rival spire. 
 Interesting worldbuilding (the humans live in Spires, ancient constructs 10,000 feet tall and 10,000 feet in diameter; the surface is a place of horrors; and most things are powered by crystals, or by electricity generated by crystals) and plenty of action, ranging from naval engagements (Napoleonic broadsides, but the ships move in three dimensions) to battles in the levels of the Spire, and more than a soupcon of intrigue and betrayal and treachery. It's billed as steampunk, but I got a bit more of an anime vibe from it -- maybe something like Last Exile or Castle in the Sky. 
 A bit of a wobbly beginning, and arguably longer than it actually needed to be, but I was entertained and will be reading the next volume when it comes out.

I have to say that I am SO happy to be done with this book. To say that it disappointed me would be somewhat of an understatement. The jacket of this book describes it as an "emotionally-charged thriller." Not at any point during this book was I thrilled, nor did I feel any emotions beyond bewilderment and anger. And what makes me sad is that it does have a promising start- I was intrigued by the beginning and invested in Shelby's story. 
 And then...it got weird. Very weird. 
 I don't want to spoil too much, but the description of this book is very misleading. If you're going into this wanting a thriller, this is not the book for you, despite what the jacket says. The jacket leaves out that about half of the book takes place in a magical dreamland, so I was totally blindsided by it. If there had even been a HINT of any of that in the description, I could have chosen not to read this book or at least been prepared. Instead, I was totally thrown off. It felt like I was reading two different books that did not go together whatsoever. Honestly, I wanted to give up when I was 150 or so pages in but I don't like to give up on books that far in. So I stuck with it, hoping it would get better...and it really didn't. The plot "twists," especially the one closer to the end that Shelby literally calls a plot twist herself, were not shocking at all. 
 The only reason I didn't give this one star, which I was really considering, is that it does have a satisfying ending. I never felt much for Shelby but I liked her character development at the end. Also, I feel like this book did a good job of representing disability, at least deafness (marked as a spoiler because you don't find out Shelby is deaf until pretty far in) . 
 I'm sure there are people out there who would enjoy this book, but if you're planning on reading it, just be prepared for what you're getting yourself into.

Warcross is a really enjoyable story to read. I get Ready Player One vibes from it and I can very well imagine seeing this on the TV screen. One star down because the final twists are quite predictable so there was no big "wow moment" for me. Otherwise, I enjoyed the whole book.

Aaaawwww maaaan. That's pretty much how I feel about this book. It was not even close to how smooth and engrossing as the first one was. It suffered from a terrible case of repetition. I will have to get into this. 
 The good: 
 1) The story, overall, was interesting and well thought through. I never knew what was going to happen next, which is pretty awesome when it comes to predictable genres likes UF. I still don't know who I would rather Mercy end up with. It's nice. 
 2) The relationships between Mercy and the rest of the characters are very fluid and well developed. She started out not liking Ben or Honey, and yet both of them turn around. I like pretty much everyone, even the "villains". It was also a plus in the first book. 
 The bad: 
 1) The repetition was horrible. I don't know how many more times I can read about dominance without rolling my eyes. I get it. No, really, I get it. Then there was the "vampires are evil...except for Stefan" bit in -every chapter-. At least once. I get it!!! And then there's the "I'm useless and everyone can kill me if they wanted to" from Mercy, over and over again. WE GET IT. 
 2) Mercy was pretty much on the sidelines for the first good 70% of the book. It just seemed like it could have been so much more. 
 I'm not going to be putting this series down for good, but it is going on the back burner for now. I will come back and read more eventually.

 I was in the mood to read a cheesy love story, one without crazy dramatic ridiculousness. I read the book synopsis, saw 'star-crossed lovers', and went for it. This is not your average paranormal love story at all. First of all, the supernatural creatures are totally original- Revenants that are kind of a mix between zombies and ghosts. I loved this idea, and totally enjoyed learning about the Revenant world. The book was laid out well, and it didn't feel like I was reading a scripted history lesson while learning their story. The pace of the book was also well thought out. It took a while before the supernatural started happening, but it was informative and interesting, instead of slow and boring like a lot of supernatural books. The action was also well-paced, not stuffed into the last fifty pages so that I was constantly flipping, trying to see what happens. I was able to take my time with the ending, and enjoyed it a lot. The setting was wonderful as well- Paris, France. What better place to set a supernatural love story?! And the Revenant world is phenomenal! I loved the originality of the Revenants themselves- the way that they died saving humans, and woke up in their bodies three days later. The way that they went dormant for three days of the month, and especially the way that they were volant- in spirit form while dormant. It was completely original and refreshing to read something new in the supernatural world! The characters were all well developed and complex. Kate is a truly wonderful character that I connected with immediately. The story began with her losing her parents in a devastating car accident and she was in a deep depression. After meeting Vincent, she was able to pull herself out of her depression slowly. Vincent is a phenomenal character- although a bit too perfect of a man for me. He is sensitive, caring, thoughtful, strong, sexy- the perfect specimen of a man, yet a bit too perfect for me. The romance between the two was done well- they took their time and didn't immediate 'fall head over heels' for each other. They weren't instantly ready to die for each other, so it was better than a lot of 'star-crossed lover' stories. My favorite part though were the supporting characters. The entire Revenant family- I fell in love with Jules and his sexy humor, Ambrose and his delicious muscles, Charlotte and her 'Alice-like' energy and enthusiasm, even Gaspard and Jean-Pierre were wonderful, complex characters. To wrap-up the first review, I totally loved this book. It was well written with original supernatural characters, thick, twisted plot-lines, and an amazing story that I cannot wait to continue!

Without You, There Is No Us by author and journalist Suki Kim is slightly different to the other memoirs by defectors. While most memoirs I have read are about conditions in the camps or dealing with daily life for the poverty-stricken lower and middle classes, this one explores the lives of the rich and 'privileged' boys being groomed to take over the North Korean administration some day. 
 Suki Kim has basically infiltrated PUST (Pyongyang University of Science and Technology), a Christian-funded university, pretending to be a missionary. In the book, she exposes both the Kim regime's dictatorship in which even the elites are brainwashed and not given any freedom, and the missionaries who lie in wait like vultures waiting to pounce on the carrion the moment the country opens up. 
 Kim's relationship with her students goes beyond the usual teacher - student relationships, partly because she is aware that their lives are restricted and feels for them, and partly because for the students, she is a major link to life on the outside. Kim describes her time with the North Korean boys, effusing her narrative with emotions, both positive and negative. The boys are completely brainwashed to the extent that they believe that North Korea is the most advanced country in the world, where they have achieved miracles such as changing people's blood types! They also believe that the axis of evil is USA, Japan and South Korea, and are forever prepared to wage war against their enemies. They are denied basic amenities like Google that we take for granted. They simply have no idea about the outside world, and one of the author's goals is to show them that there is a life outside NK and to get the boys start questioning their system. She does this by simple and sly techniques by obliquely mentioning some developments they were not privy to earlier, by keeping her Mac book in sight, and so on. 
 If the North Korean regime blocks information to the students, restricts their lives and brainwashes them, the missionaries deny them simple and basic pleasures such as a screening of a Harry Potter movie, because it's not Christian. We all know that the Kim regime is bad, but this was no less cruel in my view. They also insist on the students learning to eat with a fork, which makes no sense, since the food served is completely different. How are they going to eat soupy ramen with a knife and fork?! I found these people extremely annoying in every aspect. The missionaries positioned in North Korea and China are doing a lot of harm. But when did they ever do anything else? I liked that the author does not spare them or see their work in NK as charity. She is well aware that their sole aim is to spread Christianity, and they don't care how they do it or about the consequences. 
 I also liked that the author contributed some personal history in the form of reminiscences of her parents' lives during the war and how they had to flee at the time. She also talked about her own memories, growing up as a child in South Korea and often makes a comparison between the north and south cultures, emphasising how far the two countries have grown apart in the past sixty years. 
 While I found the book informative and enjoyable, there were some annoying elements. Kim's Americanism shows through when she keeps wondering about USA and how things are different here. Well, why wouldn't they be? US isn't a prototype for the rest of the world! Every place is different, and thrusting in America as the global standard really annoyed me. Another thing I found bizarre was that Kim would mention her lover consistently throughout the book, without us ever getting to actually know him. He was irrelevant but she would bring him up at every opportunity. Even when discussing something as trivial as a textbook passage on New York, a mention of Brooklyn would bring out a couple of random sentences about her absent lover. I would make this a full five star, if this lover had been edited out completely.

I'm a huge fan of Chelsea Cain's Sheridan/Lowell books so when I heard she was kickstarting a new series (yes that was on purpose!) I was extremely excited. It engulfed me in two mad reading sessions (one of which I only stopped because my eyes would literally not stay open a moment longer) as I pretty much inhaled the whole tale start to finish. 
 Kick Lannigan has a dark past - when she was young she was kidnapped and lived a horror story for many years until she was rescued. These days Kick is pretty sure she can look after herself as she has spent years training herself in the art of self defence and offence. When the enigmatic Bishop arrives in her life and pretty much forces her to help him track down a child recently missing, she will need all these skills and then some in order to survive and perhaps save that childs life. 
 Chelsea Cain has always managed to walk the fine line between violence, thrills and spills and emotional resonance, whilst still making the story endlessly exciting, always compelling and never ever dull. This is no exception - if anything I would say that I already prefer the nuances and background in this new series. Kick is an amazing character to follow along with, as she manages her anxiety, tries to remain always clear headed in the face of adversity and still maintain an image of strength. Not always quite managing it, she is fascinating to behold. Add to the mix tough guy Bishop, who has demons of his own, and you have a partnership that just pops off the page and will hold you in the grip of reading madness until the final moments. 
 An intelligent fast moving plot barely gives you time to catch a breath, there is a dark heart here dealing as it does with child abduction and abuse, but still having that edge of hope and redemption as we see what true survival really is...and as we race towards the finale it is heart stopping stuff. The ending was perfect (although I need to ask about the 3 legged dog...Ms Cain?) and rounds off Kick's first (one assumes) foray into a new life whilst leaving you desperate for more. 
 Perfectly done. Kudos. 
 When will there be more? 
 Highly Recommended for fans of Thriller's with an edge.

 After seeing so many bloggers rave about We Should All Be Feminists, I decided to check it out from the library and read it and see what all the fuss was about. Even though it ultimately didn't really present with anything new, I still enjoyed reading it. 
 This is an incredibly quick, short read. At just under 50 pages, it can easily be read in one sitting. Not only is it short, but the language is very accessible and not dense like a lot of nonfiction tends to be. I was able to read this in just about a half hour. 
 I have to admit, though, that this really didn't give me any new information. As someone who has identified as feminist for several years, I already knew a lot of what the author discusses here. She talks about the way in which men are often assumed to have money whereas women are not, the stigma attached the word "feminism," the gender wage gap, etc. It was all stuff that I already knew about. If you're just getting introduced to feminism, this is a great start. But if like me, you're already familiar with the topic and issues, it's unlikely it'll teach you anything new. 
 The only exception to that were the Nigerian cultural examples. I know very little (aka nothing) about Nigeria, so I did like that the author included examples of what it's like to be a woman there. There was a good mix of Nigerian and the more typical US/UK examples. 
 All in all, We Should All Be Feminists is a nice introduction to feminism and an enjoyable, quick read. But if you're someone who has been learning about feminism for awhile, I wouldn't expect to be introduced to anything new here, aside from some examples of sexism in Nigeria. Despite it not teaching me anything, I still really enjoyed reading it and I look forward to reading more by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie in the future.

 Set in the far future, the story is told in the first person point of view by U.N. Takeshi Kovacs. In this future world, people have "stacks" implanted in their brains. At intervals, people can upload their personalities and memories into a central repository. When a person dies, as long as his stack is undamaged, his memories can be reinstalled into another body, in a procedure known as "sleeving". As a result, some people live on for hundreds of years, gaining wealth, power and influence over their lifetimes. On the other hand, punishment usually consists of a temporary death, so that when reborn, a prisoner is awakened into a world that has passed him by. 
 Kovacs is reborn into the body of a disgraced policeman, on the condition that he help an ancient man solve a mystery. Why did the old man seem to commit suicide? Did he really commit suicide, and if so, what was his motive? Or, more likely, who set up his death to look like a suicide, and how? Kovacs is a very powerful guy, but that does not prevent him from getting into lots of trouble as he tries his best to solve the mystery. He is swept from one violent encounter to the next, not understanding the forces that are treating him like a pinball. 
 This story is definitely not for squeamish readers. It has graphic descriptions of violence, torture and sex. Those sections of the story really put me off. 
 Also, this type of science fiction has a logical non-sequitur that bothers me a great deal. When a consciousness is injected into another body after death, it seems to me that the person has really and truly died. The body that has his consciousness is simply another person with the same memories; how can there be any real continuity in the person's consciousness? In this story, this dilemma is examined from a weird angle; the main character's consciousness is injected into two separate bodies, and the two of them have to decide who is to die, and who is to live on. After much discussion using logic and justice, they finally decide who is to live on, by playing rock-paper-scissors!

He does very little to adjust his voice and accent to help the listener identify the speakers during the dialogs. I also must mention that Tantor Audio should be ashamed of the low quality of the audio recording. It is very quiet. They should hire recording engineers who are better at their job, and they should also do some quality control.

Definitely, Maybe in Love, by Ophelia London, is a modern day, new adult take on Pride and Prejudice. I wasn't sure what to think before I began because, on one hand, the reviews from friends were mixed, but on the other, it's P&P. I landed somewhere in the middle. 
 I enjoyed most of the differences in the characters and especially the witty banter. Henry Knightly was a smart man, not nearly as reticent or awkward as Darcy, and I liked his more straightforward approach to pursuing Spring, London's rewrite of Elizabeth Bennet. Spring was a bit overzealous with her dedication to the environment and her pursuit of standing out in a sea of students, so I can understand why she wasn't universally liked by readers. I have to admit that the parallels between Elizabeth and Spring were a little harder to make out at times. The sister relationships were replaced by friends, Julia as Jane, and Anabel as Lydia. Melanie was a rewrite of Charlotte Lucas. I found all three to be good representations of their predecessors. Melanie especially was spot on. Julia was a quintessential Jane save for her closeness with Spring. I missed their intimacy. On the male side of things, Wickham's counterpart here was Alex, and he was just as big a dick. Dart as Mr. Bingley was also a perfect fit. It wasn't clear whether Tyler was supposed to be a Mr. Collins-esque replacement--though I admit I've always found him ridiculous so I don't know his character as well as others. He didn't seem to try as hard, nor did he pursue anyone but Melanie. 
 I thought the writing was strong. The dialogue was also well done. London did a good job giving the story the same feel and following the major plot points with modern twists. I didn't love every twist though. Julia's behaviour in the climax seemed out of character, though admittedly a modern take on the Lydia situation. And while I saw Alex as a slime ball, leaving marks on a woman seemed a titch too far from the original. Most of all, I hated that Dart and Henry weren't able to 'save' Julia from drunken stupidity, only pick up the pieces.  
 Rating this book came down to one thing for me: the relationship between Henry and Spring. Regardless of the characterizations and plot differences, the attraction between our Darcy and Elizabeth wannabes mirrored the original quite nicely. I felt the pulls and pushes, the coming-togethers and falling-aparts. So that's who I'll recommend this book to: people who fell hard for the unlikely love between two seeming opposites.

 World building is as much of an art as it is a science. The premise for Gilded Cage is that the Commoners must serve the Equals (Skilled) in servitude, i.e. slavedays (it's actually one word) for ten years. YET they get to choose when they serve their years. They are allowed to move their possessions into storage during those ten years. Commoners also get to choose when to serve their days out. For instance, a Commoner can serve their years out when they are a senior citizen... how does that make for an effective slave? (I know how terrible that sentence sounds and I apologize. I don't know how else to phrase it.) While serving out their days, the Commoners who are minors receive no education, which makes this world fall apart. How can they after completing their days be successful? How can this world thrive? How does one even afford to get a car or a house before their servitude or even afterwards? Why are the Hedleys so surprised when they arrive at Kyneston and Millmoor? Do released slaves not talk, or are all the slaves put under the Silence and are unable to talk. 
 Millmoor is the slave town in which Luke finds himself. It's divided into zones. But little is know about each zone or what kind of factory work Luke does. Millmoor is a flat landscape that is written to be hell but I don't feel the hell that Luke is in at all. The problems are glossed over like that of a small skirmish written in a history book. The brutality comes off as Keystone Cop inspired. It appears that the slaves are paid in some way because there are shops for them to purchase goods. This is where my confusion comes in again, yes the Skilled wouldn't want the burden of caring for all the Commoners for ten years because it would eat into their resources and profits, but at the same time, money no matter how little gives autonomy to their slaves. 
 The language is uncomfortable at times... I cringed in upon myself like a turtle retreating into its shell. 
 "Greedy Daddy! She pinched his cheek indulgently and whispered in his ear." 
 I can't let this one go. It gives the air that Bouda has an inappropriate relationship with her father. 
 "Down on the chamber floor Dawson was up on her hind legs, yapping way. 
 So... Dawson is a dog now? I didn't know humans had hind legs. 
 Yet, there were strong passages that made me connect the book to the turmoil in today's society. 
 "You have to--hate them," the man grated out. 
 "To beat them." 
 "I don't hate them enough to kill children," Luke said, with no hesitation. 
 "Then you don't hate them--enough." 
 Unfortunately, these moments of clarity were far too few. I believe books have the power to change minds and bridge the great divide, and having a character such as Luke stand up and say that needed to be such a bigger part of this novel. 
 Abi and Luke's knowledge of the Skilled powers are rudimentary. They grow up in this world but seemed awed by it. Do the Skilled keep their powers secret? Aren't there rumors about what they can do? Aren't there any public displays or skirmishes between the Skilled and the Commoners in public? I am baffled by this. A Skilled's power appears to take shape in a variety of ways but it's never really explained how it manifests. We see the pain it brings upon the Commoners in the form of gut wrenching pain, but not an actual explanation as to what is actually happening, which really hurt the plot. 
 If the slaves are prevented from speaking about their experience then to me the fight for abolition goes belly up. How do pro-abolitionists get those who aren't serving their slavedays to care? 
 What Gilded Cage lacks is the terror and the atrocity that the Skilled inflict upon their slaves. While reading this it felt like I was stuck in the worst job I've ever worked, soul defeating but bearable. That was until I encountered the character of Dog. Here is a man who is broken and turned into a thing. This is what I wanted Gilded Cage to be. The horror of what a society built upon slavery does, not cotton candy fluff sprinkled with bits of moldy fruit cake.

Mori Phelps has always known there is enchantment in the world. She and her twin sister used to play among the fairies in the Welsh countryside, until the magical battle with their half-mad mother which killed Mori's twin. Mori herself is sent into the care of her estranged father, who sends her to boarding school, a cold and unfriendly place. Yet Mori finds refuge in her books and her journal, and in a circle of friends she discovers, perhaps by magic. 
 I loved so many things about this book that I hardly know where to begin, and I feel as though I'm preaching to the choir because I know so many people have already read and liked this. However, but what the hell, I loved it enough that I want to talk about why. I think all of Jo Walton's books are wonderful, but this might be the most wonderful. (Until the next book, quite possibly, since I think I've said this about previous books of hers.) 
 I have a thing for boarding school stories, and this one was beautifully subversive and realistic: Mori herself compares it unfavorably with Malory Towers, my own seminal boarding school story series. I liked the magical system, where magic happens in ways indistinguishable from reality, and how Mori has to grapple with that, with whether the magic she has worked has created the community she seeks or whether it was truly already there. I loved the community itself, the speculative fiction-loving community which I consider my community also. 
 And most of all, I loved the book's engagement with books, its acknowledgement of the importance of books: as Mori says, "If you love books enough, books will love you back."
Heartbreaking. If you read the series you should definitely read this novella in between!

Suspenseful and smart, Armentrout has you on the edge of your seat and will not let you move. 
 When Sasha returns to her home town she left behind ten years ago, she thinks her life will finally start to fall into place as she imagined before tragedy struck her life. When Sasha was just a teenager she was abducted by a serial killer known as "The Groom". She was the only one to escape his clutches and has spent years in intensive therapy as a result. Despite this, Sasha is a strong woman. At 29, she is still coping with her past, but has the tools to help herself now. 
 Sasha has returned to help her Mom run their family inn when strange things start to happen... Her car is broken into and girls are starting to go missing once again. The circumstances have Sasha wondering if this is coincidence or something more sinister. 
 I absolutely love when Jennifer L. Armentrout puts pen to paper.... or is it finger to keyboard now? Who knows. Jenn, how do you write, so I can get my life straight? Anyway, JLA just writes books that I want to read. She is truly such a versatile author. YA, NA, Adult - nothing can get in her way as far as content, readability, and the overall entertainment value of her novels. I would not be worried in the least to purchase any of her works. I mean she wrote about aliens in high school and it was a New York Times bestseller. Till Death is no exception to this statement. This book is one of my first 5 star reviews this year. It is suspenseful and has you on the edge of your seat trying to figure out what is going on in this town. 
 Sasha has quite the support system. Her mom and best friend are there for her any time she may need them and now Cole is back in the picture. She is reluctant at first to give into his advances, but her best friend and Mom are right there to put her back in her place. We really see Sasha grow as a character from the beginning of this book until the end. I love when books show you how the characters morph into stronger people as the story goes on. 
 This book has the perfect balance of suspense and romance. If you're worried about the romance aspect, worry not! Cole is super swoonworthy. ;) 
 If you like suspense, romance, thrillers, JLA, or all 4 you should pick up this book. You won't be disappointed. Till Death grips you from the start and keeps you locked on until the last page. Wonderful job, Armentrout, as always.

I almost skipped writing a review on this book because I'm not exactly sure how I feel about it. It took me, like, half the book to get invested in it at all. Beginnings are sometimes slow, so I'll let it pass as a non-issue, especially because half a graphic novel isn't actually all that much story wise. After that boring beginning part, though, we start getting more of the meat of the story and it becomes less of a book to finish and more of a book to enjoy. 
 The story is rather unique. I've never read anything like it before. There's zombies, vampires, ghosts, et cetera but not even close to the normal way they're usually displayed in movies and books. I feel like this book has a solid basis for how all these paranormal creatures come to be and that makes me like it a lot and want to continue with the series. Trust me, they're not present for the reasons you think they are. Not in this book/series, at least. 
 The story is told through the point of view of Gwen, who is, if you haven't guessed already, a zombie. She has to eat a brain a month to keep from turning into a shambling, mindless zombie like the ones we are all accustomed to. That's where it's really interesting. Our culture isn't used to seeing intelligent zombies (well, maybe yours is, but mine isn't), but Gwen still seems very much human with a weird predicament. "Seems" being the keyword because she is, in fact, not a living human anymore. (No plot twists there, friends. Sorry.) Gwen's a pretty likable character and I'm really looking forward to seeing what else happens in her life. 
 There's also Ellie, the ghost, who died several decades in the past. I love, love, love Ellie and seriously hope there will be lots more of her in future books. Because even though Gwen is cool, Ellie is totally my favorite. She's so sweet. Not to mention I love her hair and all the clothes she's always dressed in. Sigh. 
 As for the artwork, it's what you'd expect in a typical color graphic novel. It's pretty, but nothing really out of the ordinary. This novel is really great about keeping it realistic and non-sexualized in the graphics... except for, of course, when they add in the gratuitous changing scene where we basically see Gwen naked. I'm not sure why it had to be so explicit (for a book, at least), but it is and the age group this graphic novel is suitable for was knocked up several years because of it. (And guys, I'm far from a prude. The nudity is nothing to someone my age. I mean it's really not that bad unless you're, like, 13 years old.) 
 As a whole I'm impressed with where this series seems to be going and I really hope it'll keep my interest into the other books. If you like stories about zombies (or other paranormal creatures) I advise you to give this series a try. It really has a very interesting take on the living dead situation.

Why has this genre gone so wrong? Dystopians were what really drew me into young adult literature, but I've had such a string of disappointments that it's making me start to wonder what I saw in young adult literature in the first place. Then again, I've read some excellent young adult novels in other subgenres, so what I really think is going on is that what started out as a promising genre turned into a trend in which everything that had the faintest whiff of "dystopia" about it was rushed to press. This book is but the latest example. Some spoilers to follow. 
 First off, there's an important point that I think needs to be driven home to any author who is thinking about writing a book in this genre: a dystopia should be built from the ground up and then peopled with characters who provide a lens for examining the dystopia. This book, like many of the other young adult novels I've read lately, misses the mark entirely. The characters in this book feel like they were plopped into the middle of the dystopia. Dystopians should be all about gradually peeling back the layers of a supposedly perfect society, so that the reader is shocked and horrified by what they see, so shocked and horrified that it makes them think long and hard about whatever aspect of society the dystopia is exploring. The characters in the dystopia should not run around talking about how awful the dystopia is--because it's not a dystopia. What makes a dystopia a dystopia is the fact that it seems to be perfect until the characters either gradually realize it isn't or until the reader does, due to the casual way in which the characters navigate their world, a world that strikes the reader as utterly foreign. 
 The Program could have done this, it really could have. There were times when I was reading it where I thought it could have provided a compelling springboard for discussing how mental health issues are treated in our society, particularly when it comes to the use of medications. It's a topic that I think needs some serious discussion. Had this book served as a means of exploring the implications of drugs for depression and how they affect those who take them, it could have been very powerful. But I didn't think the book did touch this topic in any real way. 
 Instead, what this book is is a romance. There's nothing wrong with that in and of itself, but I wish that these books would label themselves more accurately. When the dystopian setting is just there to complicate the romance, I'm not interested. It's not to say that the premise of the book is without merit, because I think that it is. Exploring what it means to lose memories--particularly those of someone you love--is an interesting topic. And if it needs to have a dystopian setting, fine. But it should be clearly labeled as a "dystomance". This is not the sort of book I want to read when I'm looking for a dystopian. When I'm looking for a dystopian, what I want is something where world-building is essential because it's meant to provide a means of dissecting something about society. 
 Another big problem I have with this book is with the love interest, James. I never connected with him. At the beginning of the book, I thought he was kind of a jerk, and I didn't like how everything he said to Sloane had a sexual component. I don't want this portrayed as "typical" teen boy behavior because not every teen boy behaves this way and, more importantly, it's not okay if they do. I felt like James treated Sloane more like an object, and that turned me off immediately. I don't like the message it sends. I'm not saying that every YA should be about perfect boys who are on their best behavior at all times, but given the number of teen girls who stay in abusive relationships or who have sex before they're ready, I really dislike the way many YA novels portray boys who mistreat their girlfriends as hot. There's nothing hot about a boy who treats his girlfriend with disrespect, just as there's nothing hot about a girl who treats her boyfriend with disrespect. My dislike for James only increased at the end of the book, and I almost quit reading because I was so angry about his character. Not that Realm is any better, really. 
 My other big issue with this book was my inability to suspend disbelief. I can buy the idea that some parents would be so desperate to save their children they'd be willing to strip those children of everything that makes them who they are, but I can't buy the premise that all parents would. There is a clear dichotomy in this book: everyone thinks the program is wonderful except for the savvy teens. Maybe this will be fleshed out and given some shades of gray in future installments, I don't know. But it should have been done in this book. I don't buy that some adult somewhere wouldn't take issue with the methods used by The Program, wouldn't be upset when their child came back to them a shell of who they once were. The dumb/absent/gullible adults are a common trope in YA, one that was rather freely abused in this book. 
 It probably goes without saying, but I'm stepping off this train here and now, and I'm going to have some serious reservations about reading any more YA dystopians in the future. Honestly, it pains me to say this because I love this genre, but I kind of hope the YA dystopian trend dies out. It's not so much that it's been overdone but that it's been repeatedly done badly.

Starting this book, it reminded me a bit of Room, though with some of its own twists: the youthful, immature narrator who has lived his entire life in a locked basement with his family, the hint of something terrible in the family's past, the question of what lies outside the only home our young protagonist has ever known.... The impression held up for me until about halfway through the book, where the author diverges from the present to give us a snapshot of what exactly happened to the family and how they ended up in the basement. From this point on, the story twists and turns and wreaks havoc on what you thought you knew about the characters. The characters are strongly developed, leaving you feeling betrayed when the story changes, as it does several times, finally leading to the truth of what the family has done to get to where they are. No matter what they might have done, all of the characters are given small moments that show their humanity and it makes them feel more real. A lot of bad shit happens in this family, and it's easy to say that the relatively happy ending doesn't fit--that they didn't get what they deserve. Maybe not, but a lot of people who do bad things don't get what they deserve in real life either. I thought the ending was true to the narrator's perspective, however. This was, after all, his family, despite their confusing relationship and despicable past. The ending, as with the rest of the story, shows how the narrator relates to his family. Overall, this book kept me interested (after a slower start) and the twists had me anxious to keep reading and find out what really happened. The story was not at all what I was expecting, and it was a very good read.

What an ending!! UNSPOKEN=WOW! 
 I will fully admit I didn't love Della's books (REBORN, ETERNAL and this one UNSPOKEN) the way I did Kylie's books (first 5 books of Shadow Falls series) yet Della's story still managed to smack me with all the feels! 
 Della Tsang, Kylie and Miranda are by far one of my favorite YA heroine trios! Always have been! They are so different yet fit together so well with the radically different personalities and chemistry. 
 Speaking of chemistry: Della and Chase! YES please :D 
 I love them so much! He's there for Della, had been from the start--despite his singularly stupid decision to keep a huge secret from Della for ages...but that was an ETERNAL plot point that carried over into UNSPOKEN. Chase changed his life for Della and really grew into a great character. 
 The love triangle that was a thing in the first two books wasn't really a thing in this one. It was Della and Chase all the way! Poor Steve................. 
 Here's my thing, though. As said above Della is not my fav of the girls so getting into her story as much as I did Kylie's and Miranda's took time. But the fact that I still came to care so damn much about Della and Chase speaks volumes to the incredible talent of C.C. Hunter as an author. 
 UNSPOKEN was a wonderful book, but not how I want the story of Shadow Falls and it's students to end. Thank GOD C.C. Hunter herself told a friend of mine--who is also a huge fan of C.C.-- that there's more possibly coming--several short stories about other characters!! YEAH!!!!! Happy dance!!!!!!!! 
 My biggest woe with UNSPOKEN was how so many of the great characters of the Shadow Falls universe--who usually manage to have a good presence in the other books--just felt thrown in for most of the book. I didn't get nearly enough of the kick butt K/D/M charlie angel's type feeling that they normally have. 
 Plus there was so much of Jenny/Derek/Perry/Miranda/Lucas/Kylie/Holiday/Burnett moments I wanted that I felt deprived. So many other great and relatable characters are in this series I can see how it can be a challenge to do them all justice and not take away from Della's story, so I kinda understand, but not really. 
 Again--this speaks to Hunter's amazing talent at creating "real" characters. She always finds the right amount of humor, romance, action, twists, drama and all around fantasticalness in each book. I wanted to hug and cry for Della so many times, I cheered for her and was not eh edge of my couch needing to see what happened next. 
 UNSPOKEN is slightly darker-mostly because of the more upfront interaction with the vampire gangs- but it's good and will please any fan of Shadow Falls with it's ending! 
 Now all that's left is to get those possible, last few short stories that should be coming down the pike, hopefully :) 
 Do I recommend this: HELL YES!!!! I recommend every single book and ebook short in the series!!

 Kellan Brooks has had it with his father's need to control his life. His dad cutting him off after he broke of his engagement was the straw that broke the camel's back. Kellan is determined to shove it in his dad's face and he's figured out the best way to do it too. Take one extremely homophobic dad with a sketchy new deal on the line and insert his brand new out and proud gay son. And the best part, the best part is Kellan is determined to use the one man who has even more reason to hate his father than he does. Kellan may have screwed up in the past with Nate, but he's gay and they used to be best friends. Kellan's sure he can convince Nate to jump on board with his plan. 
 The last thing Nate Gray ever expected to hear out of his straight ex-friends mouth is the four words that cam pouring out. "I need a boyfriend." After being betrayed by Kellan as a teen and taunted all those years for being gay Nate isn't exactly receptive to Kellan's plight. It's been thirteen years since he had anything to do with the guy and now he's begging Nate to play along in his little scheme. Playing a game of gay chicken with a gay man though is never a smart idea and suddenly what started as a taunt is becoming way to real. 
 Ok so Nate can be a very self-absorbed jerk sometimes, but I have to admit to really liking Kellan despite his playboy tendencies. Despite being a trust fund baby Kellan buckles down and doesn't complain about having to work a menial day job. He's going to do what he has to do to stay afloat and not be under his dad's thumb. He has a good heart, unwilling to have other people hurt because he dad is still trying to control his life. And ultimately he finds a lot of his happiness helping out those less fortunate than himself. Whatever his confusion over his sexuality underneath it he's a good guy. Plus he knows how to have fun, something Nate seems to be sorely lacking at times. Most of the time Nate still comes across as an old stick in the mud fuddy-duddy. 
 I did appreciate how guilty Nate was feeling over his initial actions in respect to Kellan. Not the coolest move on his part, though Nate, being Nate, does obsess over it for a bit longer than is strictly necessary. For an out gay man Nate doesn't really know what he wants. He's got very limited views and needs Kellan's outrageousness to shake him out of his routine. Kellan has his reasons for his own screwed up behavior, but he seems much more willing to take a chance on what makes him happy. 
 Of course the sex is hot and Eli is adorable so the second half of the book gets much more entertaining. I giggled at Eli's descriptions of things that almost send Kellan running for the hills. What a way to screw up a questioning guys brain...describe gay sex. :D But yes Eli is the cutest thing since sliced bread (for a really terrible, wrongly used--bread cute?? but I don't care, cliche) . 
 The history between these two guys makes the flow of the story easier to get behind. There's a lot they already know about each other and it's more about rediscovering that what made them friends to begin with is still there between them. Just with an added new sexy element thrown in. For me it makes the speed within which everything happens a little more believable. 
 Altogether this is a lot of dramatic mental head spinning thrown into a quick story, but it still works for me. I'd probably give this a 3.5 stars overall rounded up to 4 as I've read this one a few times now and always enjoyed it.

 My Life with the Walter Boys and I had a turbulent time to say the least. I don't know if it was my mood, my frame of mind or just the fact that it drove me up the bloody wall but this review will show you why we didn't work together. It's not going to be pretty or carefully constructed. This review will be short and to the point because that's what you guys need to see to decide whether you want to try it. 
 There isn't much of a plot, just what it says on the tin. Jackie's life with the Walter boys. That's all. Once I'd finished the book (that's right, I stuck it out!) I went onto Goodreads to see what others thought of it and I honestly have no idea what went wrong. So many readers loved it, even bloggers that have a similar taste in books as me. 
 The characters were one-dimensional without any spark whatsoever. In fact, there were way too many secondary characters to keep track off and remember. They were picked up and dropped when it was necessary to the plot. The conversations were stilted and awkward. At one point, Jackie says to her ex, "I can't forgive you yet, the wound is too raw" but then she watches a movie with him and oh hey, they're back together again. Guess that wound healed pretty sharpish, huh? 
 Another thing is that Walter parents don't say a word. They let their kids run riot, they are nowhere to be seen half the time. Not even a word in Jackie's ear to stop messing their boys about. 
 Scenes were glossed over. This is one of my major pet peeves. Even worse is when the next paragraph is a backtrack to explain how Jackie suddenly has this extra knowledge she didn't have in the last chapter. If it's important, write it out. Don't skip over it and then cover your tracks 
 It wasn't all bad though. There were brief moments I found amusing but the bigger picture felt like a I was watching a really bad slapstick comedy. 
 My Life with the Walter Boys has a lot of potential but to come anywhere near achieving it, it needs a really good edit, an overhaul of the cliches and more showing rather than telling.

I'm writing this review after my....5th reading of this book? Give or take. 
 I first read The Mediator series in 2009 at my mother in laws insistence. I love this series so much that I actually read the series at least 3 times back to back to back. 
 Basic premise: Suze Simon is a mediator - she can see, speak to, and touch ghosts. Her job is to help them resolve their unfinished business and move on to whatever comes next. 
 This book doesn't see as much Jesse (the ghost who haunts Suze's bedroom) as I'd like, but the ending is SO worth it! 
 Suze is her hilarious self, forced to work a summer job (her first ever!) as a hotel babysitter. The worst part for her? The lack of fashion. Forced to wear a one piece bathing suit and khakis. And oh yeah, the seventeen year old brother of the kid she's forced to babysit day after day is totally into her and won't take NO for an answer. 
 Meanwhile at home, her stepfather Andy, and Dopey (her stepbrother, real name Brad) are digging a hole in the yard for a hot tub, and happen to dig up a skeleton, roughly 150 years old. 
 And Suze freaks because who else would be buried in her backyard than her beloved Jesse, who was murdered roughly 150 years ago? Surely now that his body has been found, he'll be at rest and no longer haunt her house. 
 I don't want to give away spoilers to those who haven't read this book, but seriously. Amazing. Suze is hilarious and so a typical sixteen year old girl. Whenever someone asks me for a new YA book recommendation, this is one of the first to roll off my tongue (along with Meg Cabot's 1-800-Missing series). There are currently six books in the series, and this one here, book four, Darkest Hour, is the kick off to the REALLY great books in the series. Great story arc. 
 Read this book. Seriously. You won't regret it.

 I've been waiting for months for Resentment, and I'm so glad I patiently waited for it. Ever since I got the chance to read a brief preview of this, I was instantly hooked for the very fact that this seemed like my cup of tea---a 
 love-hate relationship

 I loved how the story was divided into three parts:

 and 
 Redemption. 
 Regret was mostly a sort-of flashback, wherein we see the initial build-up of the relationship between Mia and Dean. Truth be told, the first division was my favorite part. 
 "Dean Collins is the most irresistible asshole at Central High School.

Everbound was so captivating. After the events of Everneath, Nikki wasn't going to give up hope. She was going to find a way to save Jack and herself. But she had no idea how and the mythology books she was piling in her room didn't have any answers. Unfortunately, Cole was last and only resort. 
 Everbound was Nikki's descent into the Everneath in search of Jack, with a mixture Egyptain and Greek mythology and hints of Dante's Inferno mixed in. There were different rings of a labyrinth that Nikki had to go through, with the help of Cole, in order to have any hope of finding Jack in the Tunnels. While I wish the story would have mirrored the myths and scenery I'm familiar with in the Underworld, I was captivated nonetheless. The Everneath was certainly unique and dangerous. 
 In order to stay focused, Nikki often reminisced about moments with Jack to keep her tether intact and her memories strong. It was her way of holding on to him. I loved getting more of their story as she searched for him. Although I never questioned the depths of their relationship, I have to admit that Cole's character grew on me. I think he really did care about Nikki and I felt bad for him. Even in the end. It was kind of heart wrenching, actually, because he helped her and forced her to hold on to memories of Jack to prevent getting lost in the Everneath, but I'm sure hearing the moments ate at him a little. 
 The ending really surprised me. I'm anxious to see what happens in Evertrue. I would recommend this series, but I will admit that it's not my favorite mythology retelling. It's kind of different, weird, and very focused on one singular action versus exploring a whole world of mythological elements. But there's something about it that drew me in and kept me interested the entire time.

This book seriously surprised me. I took it for a slightly silly, albeit fun, pseudo-horror story with loads of references to my favourite decade. As far as the 80's quips it didn't disappoint and the story WAS fun and even silly at times. But that ending. I never would have guessed that this would end with one of the most poignant portrayals of friendship that I would ever read or that I would end up sitting on my couch and blubbing like a baby during the final chapter. 
 Abby and Gretchen have been best friends since they were 10 when they bonded over a shared love of ET and The Go-Gos. These two are true BFF's and do absolutely everything together. Fast forward six years and the fateful night that everything changed. The girls and some friends decide to give drugs a try and as they're waiting around for the drug to take effect, Gretchen wanders off and gets lost in the woods. When she doesn't come back, Abby frantically searches for her all night. Whilst out traipsing through the trees she finds an abandoned hut type thing that spooks her. She later finds Gretchen there in the morning and though Gretchen isn't quite herself, they assume it's just the aftermath of the drug and they head home. But strange things start happening to Gretchen and it's obvious that something very bad happened to her that night in the woods. She starts on a downward spiral of weird behaviour and alienates everyone except Abby. Abby is the only person that takes these changes in Gretchen seriously and tries everything she can to get her friend help but no one else seems to think there is a problem. Suddenly Gretchen seems to snap out of it--she's radiant and exciting and now everyone wants to be her friend. But Abby can see through it and knows that the Gretchen she knows and loves is gone. She enlists the help of an exorcist to bring her friend back from wherever she is before it's too late and she loses her forever. 
 I highly recommend this to readers that like a quick and fun read, campy horror and are like, totally into gnarly 80's references. And if you haven't talked to your best friend today, go and call her immediately.

Ok, per usual, I'm going to talk about the whole damn series (at least up to book 5, since that's all that exists at this point). If this is a problem, feel free to not read this. 
 So its actually been a couple of months since I read this series, but I yesterday I had a conversation about these books and I thought I'd put down my thoughts. 
 Firstly, I like this series. Please keep that in mind as we continue. I like that the characters are flawed and interesting and develop over the course of the series. I like that the only "good" and "incorruptable" character was killed in the first book. Frankly, that's what you get for being an idealist who can't or won't compromise. No one likes a self-righteous do-gooder telling them how to be morally straight. And if you can't play politics, you should stay the hell out. Particularly if you live in a world where politics = assassinations. 
 However, Martin seriously needs a draconian editor. These books are TOO LONG and TOO DETAILED. I love that he wants us to be in his world with him and that he wants his world to be rich and detailed. However, I don't need everyone's back story. I don't need the detailed version of the trip up the Vail. The Reader's Digest version will suffice, thanks. Also, I don't need a blow by blow of every battle that occurs. I could give two shits about who slew who in Rob's battles. Give me the results and the tricky moves. Otherwise, spare me every sword blow. Yes, I am aware that some people like this shit, and no, I just don't care. Also, I don't need the details of all of Daenyrus' battles either. Just give me the updates and the interesting bits like when Tyrion set the river on fire. 
 So the conversation I had yesterday got me to thinking. My friend's husband, Eddie, said that he had read some feminist critiques of this series and he basically laughed at their complaints. We had a discussion about how he thinks that since fantasy is loosely based off our own medieval times that he wants "realism" in gender and race relations. I told him that was a load of shit and that its a FANTASY and the author can do whatever he wants with the world. There is no need for fantasy worlds to be a reflection of our own history when the author can literally craft any damn thing they want. Eddie was having no part of this argument and wanted a reason that women wouldn't have been oppressed in a fantasy world. So, this is for Eddie: 
 1. There are fucking DRAGONS. Why is this important? Because man isn't an apex predator anymore. People are being hunted and eaten just like other animals. If you don't think that this changes how society develops then you my friend are an idiot. Its not like we can build walls and keep those fuckers out, they can swoop down at any time and eat anyone they want to. This changes how society develops because we need every single person defending the villages, not just able bodied men. In this kind of society women are expected to take up arms and learn to use a bow/arrow and sword just like men. It gets hard to oppress a part of your society that is armed and that you NEED armed. And when women are an integral part of your survival they can't just be devalued to being something to fuck and to pop out babies. 
 2. There is fucking MAGIC, and women can wield it. Please see Melissandre for all the evidence I need for this. If one woman in this universe can use such strong magic than it would be odd if there weren't others. And if you want to know why this changes society to stop the oppression of women please see my above entry about women having power. Also, I know for sure that it isn't just Melissandre who has magic, the witch that Danny saved had the power to sacrifice Danny's child and keep Drago alive. That's some kind of power. 
 Now for speculation on how ANY fantasy world could "account" for women never being subjugated. I still don't know why wanting to write a book that uses that theme as a way to reflect on our on societal development isn't valid, but here we go anyway. 
 1. There are lots of diseases in our own world that show up more in men than women. Perhaps in our fantasy world this is MUCH more prominent. You could make your own version of hemophilia or debilitating autism. Men who bleed out or who can't interact with others would make for poor soldiers. If the rate is even as high as 1 in 3 than you're going to have a society that depends on women to rule, make decisions, and defend their kith and kin. 
 2. Dragons respond to smell and perhaps they respond better to female pheromones. If you have a society where the women can tame the dragons but men can't get near them then you have changed the power balance. Again, its hard to opress a segment of the population that can have their pets roast and eat you. 
 3. Maybe religion never developed in this society. A LOT of our preconceived notions of gender and gender roles derive from religions. And while not all religions are patriarchal the majority of them in our world are. If there isn't a god (or gods) who are telling men that they are in charge of women, maybe men as a whole don't decide that women don't matter. 
 4. Women came up with religion and birth/creation is revered. Or maybe women are the only ones who can commune with the god figure. (Think greek priestesses but without the crazy priests). Or maybe because women were involved in birthing the religion they are frequently in positions of power in the religion. If you are used to seeing a woman standing in front of you telling you what is right it would be weird to think that you don't have to listen to a woman's opinion. 
 I could go on, but I won't. I'm sure there are a bazillion more ways to "justify" different gender stereotypes and roles. I still don't think that its necessary, but sure, you want a back story I'll give you a back story. 
 All of that being said, however, Eddie was right about one thing: the critiques he read were flawed and full of crap. Martin actually does a really good job with having and developing interesting female characters in this series. While Sansa is exactly the type of character that feminists hate (myself included), she's really the only main female character who is a self absorbed victim. And honestly, don't we all know this girl? She's vain and silly and doesn't seem able to cope with the drastic changes that are happening around her. She's a great foil for her sister and every other character in the book. She's the absolute worst of femininity and when she isn't pissing me off (never) she's a wonderful reminder about female fears of what we would be like in a crisis. 
 Every other female character in this series is strong and interesting and resilient. Danny starts as a victim (and I didn't like her) and becomes a leader. She changes her circumstances by force of will. And frankly, she was a little girl when the books started, as she ages she gets more complex and stops letting people run all over her. She's also head strong and beautifully unsure. I think she's my favorite character in the books because she is so complex. And despite the strength, she is an attractive woman. I mention this because feminist criticism frequently laments that women are never portrayed as both beautiful AND strong. Well, Martin's got you here, ladies. 
 Cersei might be the strongest female character in the series. Admittedly, she's a bit nuts and gets worse as we go on, but she sure doesn't bend to anyone. She's ambitious and only cares for herself. She doesn't listen to men (or anyone) and she doesn't take shit from them once Robert is dead. Yea, she might be evil, but you can't tell me she wouldn't do well on Wall Street. She's the medieval version of Gordon Gekko but with a focus on power rather than money. She fails for the same reason that Ned Stark fails: she's too unable to bend. Ned was too good and she's too evil. People who can't compromise can't win, end of story. 
 Ygritte and Brianne are both strong females who fight along side men. Both are out of the mainstream society, but both win love and affection from the readers and other characters. Ygritte seems happier with her life, but Brianne was able to choose her life and make her own way. 
 Ariya and Catherine Stark are also complex characters who don't fit the victim role. Ariya has more adventures than most boys her age and while she depends on men to save her (see the assassin that she saves from death only to have him get her out of servitude), she also depends on her own determination and wits. Catherine takes initiative and is a good negotiator. She knows the power players and people actually listen to her counsel. She's feminine, a mother and a fierce fighter (at least behind the scenes). And until she is killed and comes back to life she is kind and mostly good. 
 All in all, Martin does well with the female cast. They are flawed and different from each other, but they are human. And some of the most interesting and engaging story lines are those of the women in the story. As a woman, I don't ask for perfection, I ask for just that.

 When a blood red comet streaks the sky the kingdoms are divided. 
 Where once one king ruled over Westeros, now the Seven Kingdoms are splintered. 
 Swords and sentiments clash over who is the rightful ruler. 
 The sequel to 'A Game of Thrones' took me longer to finish - and not just because of its greater length - but I left it just as eager for the next installment. I once again listened to the book on audio, and it was definitely Roy Dotrice's excellent narration that helped keep hooked. 
 Martin is a master at world building, and while his cast of characters is vast and I frequently struggled to keep some of the lesser characters' names and roles straight, I became invested in the journeys and conflicts of the book. 
 'A Clash of Kings' continues the same point of view characters as the first installment, minus that slain, with two new additions: Davos the Onion Knight, a member of Stannis' court, and Theon Greyjoy, an established secondary character. Despite finding Theon to be a repugnant character, I was more engaged in his story-line than Davos', despite the latter being a far more sympathetic and level-headed character. 
 It was interesting to have an introduction to Stannis' character, as he was only alluded to in 'A Game of Thrones.' He is the quintessential jaded middle child. While not likable, his bitterness is well rooted and understandable. 
 My favourite characters remain to be Tyrion Lannister and Arya Stark. Arya's journey guised as a boy was a compelling and tense one. She definitely grew in such hostile and erratic surroundings. Tyrion is a fascinating character. He values intelligence over brute strength but also willing to face battle when the situation proves most dire. His is a peculiar character, as his allegiance is so tightly bound to his blood, even when several of his family members are so poisonous toward him. 
 Martin is skilled at raising the stakes, and always teases at several paths a character's journey may take, but never settling on the easy route. The novel ends at many turning points for the POV characters and I look forward to seeing where they lead in the next installment, 'A Storm of Swords.'

The Survival Kit is written for the readers who painstakingly shy away from issue novels; from the inevitable pain and hurt and pure emotion that they bring. While Freitas's novel is beautifully written, capturing the emotions of grief and heartache in a seamless manner and integrating within this story a romance that is both deep and palpable, the inevitable "punch" that is common to most grief novels - you know, that moment when it seems as if the wind has been knocked out from you and the floor has fallen beneath you and all of a sudden your vision is blurry with pooling tears - never comes. Unfortunately, sometimes all I want is a real kick to my gut; a true feeling that reminds me that my life isn't all that bad, that my own feelings don't matter in the realm of this book or this character. Although The Survival Kit evidently deliver in the way I wanted it to, I can't say that I've regretted a single moment I spent with this breathtaking novel in my hands. 
 Arguably, the beginning of this novel is the weakest. Although its first few pages are gripping - a funeral, a dead mother, a survival kit put together by a dying mother to help her daughter cope - the following chapters are forgettable. As is Rose, our main character. Until, that is, the story suddenly picks up and before I knew it, the pages were flying beneath my fingertips. While Rose is inscrutable and hidden to us at first, after the initial slow start, she slowly blooms, opening up to the reader and becoming strikingly real. Not only does her narration become far more accessible, de-cluttering from the previous tiresome passages of description or introspective boredom, but her journey truly begins as well. Once Rose begins to take that first peek into the survival kit her mother made her - full of items such as an iPod, a star, or a box of crayons - and then makes the conscious decision to survive life, not just get by, I began to love her. Honestly, there is nothing I love more than a protagonist who is willing to take her future into her hands and mold it. While Rose was still grieving heavily, unable to return to cheerleading or listen to music, I love that she allowed others to help her. Whether it was her grandmother who became her rock to lean on or her best friend, Krupa, who lent her her hand and shoulder whenever she needed it, Rose slowly began to emerge from the shroud of depression. 
 As a character, Rose is three-dimensional and real, never succumbing to unnecessary drama and proving to be every bit as real with others in her life as she is with the reader. And while her support system is incredible, that doesn't mean her life isn't falling apart. For one, her father has resorted to drinking away his problems, unable to cope with the death of his wife. Furthermore, her older brother, Jim, is struggling in his own way. While Rose was able to slowly handle her mother's death on her own and with the help of her friends, seeing her come to a full circle and help her family heal together was a touching journey. All too often, grief novels neglect others in their portrayal of one individual's grief, but I'm glad that Freitas gave ample attention to the grief of a father, a son, and a daughter with this one. Furthermore, Rose is not the only grieving character in our tale. Enter: Will. As the gardener in Rose's home, Will has been overlooked quite often - until he suddenly isn't. For me, the greatest strength of this novel lies within its love story. Will and Rose's blooming romance is slow, deliberate, and utterly adorable. Seriously, the swoons and "aww!"s will just keep coming when it's about these two. And yet, their relationship was real and went through hurdles that were realistic, not contrived. All the more, Will becomes a truly in-depth character as well, proving to be more than just the love interest of our tale. Freitas's integration of both the romance and self-growth in this novel was beautifully rendered, all with the theme of the survival kit in the background. 
 Still, not all is perfect in this novel. Honestly, I can forgive a novel for a slow start, but what I cannot forgive are the mixed feelings. As I mentioned before, I was seeking a punch with this one - one that never came although I expected it to. Additionally, though, I felt as if some aspects of Rose's life were just too convenient. For one, her cheerleading friends - and Krupa - were supportive all the time and while this is ideal, it isn't realistic. As much as we'd all like to be that perfect friend, life happens. We have good days, we have bad days, we have days when we can't deal with a moping, depressed friend, no matter how bad their life is. For me, these friends were rocks for Rose, but never characters in their own right. Where was their depth? Furthermore, Rose's mother is also cast as an angelic figure in this book. And although I understand the need to create a perfect image of a deceased person, the truth is, people are not perfect. And I doubt Rose's mother was too. What happened to the classic mother/daughter arguments that are characteristic of teen years? Where was the guilt, the anger, the betrayal? Surely, not all of that could have been lost simply because Rose's mother had cancer. For me, small aspects like this one went a long way into making the overall impact of this novel suffer. 
 The Survival Kit, though, is one of the rare beauties that contemporary has to offer. On a rainy afternoon like this one, Donna Freitas managed to capture - and hold - my attention long enough for the pages of her unexpectedly little-known novel to pass by. And although The Survival Kit is not perfect and often left me swinging between feelings of pure elation from one minute and disappointment to the next, I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it. Not at all.

 Guys, this book was so addictive. I knew I needed to stop reading and go to sleep but I just couldn't. I needed to know what was going to happen. Every time I thought I would read just one more chapter, something would transpire that had me clutching the book to find out if everything turned out okay. I just couldn't stop. 
 Mia was a great heroine, but she will frustrate you. What makes Mia great is that she could be anyone. She is a 25 year old and basically dealing with a quarter life crisis. She doesn't really know what she wants from life. What she thinks she wants she really doesn't and she wants what she thinks she shouldn't. It's all really confusing. It also makes her frustrating but not necessarily in a bad way. You have to remember that as a reader its easy to see the choices she should make but if you were living it you could see why she made the choices she did make. I think it's safe to say that most people go through a period where they don't really know what they want. A time when they think they have it all planned out only to find out that it's not what you expected. As a 24 year old who is still pretty new to the real world, I know I connected with Mia. Although if I had Will, let's just say I would have jumped on that a lot quicker. 
 Will *sigh* some of my favorite characters are named Will (Cooper, Herondale) and this Will is no different. Will Ryan is amazing and I fell hard for him. Let's not even talk about the fact that he is a musician, because that's really just icing on the cake. Will is just; I can't even put him into words. He is emotional and lives life to the fullest. He wears his heart on his sleeve and loves unconditionally. He is just amazing. Its why your heart will break for him, because while he is sure in what he wants, Mia is still trying to find herself. 
 Like I said, I couldn't put this book down. I just kept reading and reading because I just needed the conclusion. I kept saying one more chapter. One more chapter will help ease my mind and then I can sleep. But with each chapter I just became more and more invested in the story and my mind never eased enough for me to stop reading. I doubted that everything would turn out okay in the end. Really its better I finished the book because I wouldn't have been able to sleep if I didn't get the conclusion. Less sleep is better than no sleep. The story made my heart hurt and my emotions run wild, but I wouldn't have had it any other way. 
 One thing I need to mention is Mia's friend Jenny. I didn't like her and her tough love crap very much. I know Mia needed to hear some unpleasant things, but that wasn't what really bothered me. Be warned, the next bit could be considered a spoiler. When Mia and Will fall apart, Jenny clearly sides with Will. I'm sorry; you don't do that to a friend. If you are friend with both people, you stay out of it, you do not take sides! Even if she was upset with the choices Mia made, if she is truly your friend you don't judge and you don't cut her off. You talk to her and see where she is coming from and explain how you feel about the situation and why you think she should have acted differently. Or if you want to remain friends with both people, which is perfectly fine, you stay out of it! Again, you do not take sides! I mean, how old are we? I don't like that she put all the blame on Mia, because in the end relationships require two people. Okay I'm done ranting. It's a shame I really liked Jenny up until then. Moving on.
