 This book wasn't terrible by any means, but I don't understand all the OMG GLOWING 5STAR THIS IS THE BEST BOOK EVER reviews. 
 The characters were, for the most part, likable and well written. I like how they both had fleshed out back stories and most of their stories were not dumped on us via weird monologues, but instead was slowly revealed over time. 
 I had some issues with the book though. At first, I really liked how Camryn was independent and interesting, but she ended up being a complete wuss. I also don't like how the author constantly had every male character (except the few good guys) turn in to a wannabe rapist. I hate that. 
 First, Camryn is at a club with her best friend. She's on the roof of the club chatting with a guy and her best friend's boyfriend shows up, beats the crap out of the guy, then tries to force himself on Camryn. Ok, he was a total douchebag and I get that. No problem. 
 Later on, Camryn is on the bus and she's chatting with Andrew. There's another guy on the bus who later tries to rape Camryn in the bathroom and she has to be saved by Andrew. 
 Okay, fine. 
 But then Andrew goes into this macho man mode that totally put me off. He tells Camryn that she can no longer travel by bus, he will not allow it. She MUST either take a plane home or go with him. She agrees. WTF? She barely knows this guy and she's letting him tell her what to do? 
 Fortunately, Andrew acts decently throughout the majority of the book so I didn't flip out too much by his "I'm the man, you will do as I say" behavior. But later on, he and Camryn have this weird conversation where he tells her that he won't have sex with her because he can't do that unless she agrees that he will own her. 
 Say what?? 
 Then Camryn starts talking about how she's sexually submissive (girl, you are submissive in EVERYTHING, not just sex) and there is this whole dominant/submissive thing that's just thrown in there and seems completely opposite to Andrew's personality throughout the rest of the entire book. 
 I also just can't stand the whole "I can't breathe without you" or "I will die without you" or "I want to own you" crap, and there is a decent amount of that. Whenever I read that kind of stuff (and there's a decent amount of it in The Edge of Never) I want to just do this: 
 (sigh) 
 I didn't have a huge problem with the reveal Andrew made at the end, though I did think it was out of nowhere and went bad way too fast. 
 Overall, the book wasn't bad. I liked the main characters (outside of those issues above and most of that wasn't commonplace in the book, it happened sporadically). The plot was interesting and the writing was decent.

I was expecting a mediocre paranormal romance with lots of unnecessary drama and annoying heroine, and which I would enjoy only because of Spade and the dialogue. Instead, I got an intense, steamy and emotional journey filled with realistic characters that sucked me right in and didn't let go until I the last sentence. Yes, there is an inexplicable, sudden attraction which apparently began before the events of this book, yes, the plot has serious flaws and yes, Denise has her moments. But hey, it's paranormal romance and without these annoying things it wouldn't be. 
 In many ways, Denise and Spade are complete opposites. She's an ordinary woman, working to earn money and trying to get herself together. He's a filthy rich vampire who enjoys life. She swore to never enter the paranormal world again because last time she did, it cost her her husband. He despises humanity because it took his lover decades ago. Yet they are also similar. They both grieve, they both feel immense guilt and they both go to sleep feeling 'if only...'. Unlike sympathetic people around them, they understand each other's pain because it is so similar to their own. That's why they can heal each other. 
 I was honestly prepared for a whiny, crying heroine. It would've been understandable. Except Denise isn't. She suffers from PTSD, she gets panic attacks and she is so damn afraid. She loathes the paranormal world. It scares her to death and all she wants is normality. She even gave up on her best friend just to never see the creatures that destroyed her happiness ever again. Yet she rushes into it again without question, bravely enters a room full of vampires, gives up pieces of her humanity to a demon and goes without sleep for days, all of this to save her family members. The only time she considers giving up is when it's Spade who might get killed instead, all because of her. Spade, on the other hand, is acting irrationally and unlike himself, scaring his friends. Spade, the gentleman who is known for seeing humans only as food and occasional shag, presents Denise as his lover in front of his whole line, enters illegal underground drug circle, lies to his friends and risks his life over and over again just to help this lovely, strong and so easily killable human. While he doesn't get a lot of development himself, Spade is a major factor in Denise's. Together they make the book work. Add some amazing friends near the end and the ride become really, really enjoyable. 
 First Drop of Crimson is full of cliches. Especially the epilogue. It is one big fat sappy cliche but do I give a damn? No. Because it is so damn sweet, and so damn good, and so damn right that I can close my eyes on everything and just enjoy the good feelings it brings. The whole book is about moving on, about learning how to forgive yourself, about realizing that second chances happen. The last couple of chapters and epilogue show exactly that and allow the reader to see how far one of the characters has come. After reading the last sentence you will be smiling, you will feel good and you will be completely satisfied. 
 And by the way, I think Frost should stick with 3rd person POV because, unlike in her main Night Huntress books, I did not have issues with her writing in this one. There are still multiple repetitions and it still isn't anything spectacular, but it didn't bother me.

This book caught my attention a lot quicker than I expected it to. I was engrossed from page one, and sped through the first half. I really enjoyed the way the characters were introduced and the glimpse into small-town Texas life. But, what I found interesting at first became almost unbearably frustrating about halfway through. The mother in the story is so unlikable and repetitive, I wondered how any of her family could even stand to be in the same room with her, let alone actually love her. Maybe it is because I'm not from the South, but I cannot imagine any teenager (let along two) allowing a parent to mess up their lives so much without fighting even a little bit. The romance was pushed way too fast without any depth added to the main characters feelings for each other. They barely have a conversation and then the reader is expected to believe they are so in love? It makes the ending seem falsely emotional. I did enjoy the main plot and its focus on the music. I believed in this band and was rooting for them to succeed. The book moved quickly and was broken up with song-lyrics, which helped to push the story along. 
 If you enjoy small-town romances (complete with purity rings!) and country music, you will probably enjoy this book. Everyone else should probably skip it.

This book reminded me of the middle parts of W.H. Auden's September 1, 1939, the bits about a society in a stupor, it's members leading lives of horror and loneliness thinly papered over with bright lights and wine. 
 I did not particularly like this book. The best of its characters are in the dark and the worst are filled with passionate intensities. Our young hero loses his mother in a terrorist bombing, his father abandons him, treats him as a means to an end, and, effectively, abandons him again. People take him in and treat him with great kindness that he repays with thoughtless cruelties and abandonments of his own. He does save a dog, which is his greatest moment of grace through most of the text. But for most of the time, he is banally cruel. 
 The MacGuffin at the heart of the book is a painting of a goldfinch, chained by the foot to a wall like the shadows in the cave or the straps on Procrustus's bed. Our young hero stole the painting in the first few pages; a sin for which he could have been forgiven had he stepped up and made good. But that is not our man's way. Things are done to him; he only rarely does, and rarer still does he do the hard, honest thing. He is no Buffy. 
 I wanted this book to grapple with it means to live after the lights go out. I wanted this book to grapple with what Auden grappled with. How do we live: 
 Uncertain and afraid 
 As the clever hopes expire 
 Of a low dishonest decade: 
 Waves of anger and fear 
 Circulate over the bright 
 And darkened lands of the earth, 
 Obsessing our private lives; 
 The unmentionable odour of death 
 Offends the September night. 
 I wanted him to treat the explosion at the museum like something that mattered. He never did. That might have been the hidden heart of this book; that our boy will not look into that heart of darkness because he cannot bear it, just like many of us do not look hard at our tragedies, personal or political. We just repeat our dysfunctions on stages large and small. 
 In the end - spoiler alert - he gets some sort of redemption, largely through the cunning, courage, and kindness of others. He even has a moment of insight, or something like it, and shows some affirming flickers. Making us feel good about our on banal, cruel pasts. Or something. 
 The book did not speak to me, but its pages turned.

A Monster Calls is a fantastic story yet so real and heartbreaking.

 It's about a yew tree. 
 It's about a monster. 
 It's about living and dying, all at once. 
 It's about healing. 
 It's about the fear of losing a loved one. 
 It's about THE NIGHTMARE. The worse bad dream you ever had. 
 I'm so glad this is my first book of the year. I'm a big crying mess right now but it's okay because tonight I'll crawl up in my bed and my mom will come to visit me in my dreams. I might even have THE NIGHTMARE again but tomorrow I'll remember stories not always have a happy ending yet if we keep going, things will be alright someday.

 A multi-generational saga and tome of a novel that reminds the reader of how much of life is a gamble and that enlightened a Westerner like me on the discrimination ethnic Koreans have faced in Japanese society for decades. Min Jin Lee is an incredible storyteller.

Oh, ancient art of letter writing, what has happened to you? 
 I occasionally have little bouts of 'I'm Going to Write People Letters' phases. These phases never last long as I run out of stamps and never feel like going to the post office to buy more. Every time I hear news about email systems it occurs to me that part of our historical record has died. Does anyone donate email records to local libraries for future historians to read? I do not know. 
 Ella Minnow Pea (say it out loud.... get it?) by Mark Dunn is a small novel about letters told through the letters of residents of Nollop. This tiny island off the coast of South Carolina only claim to fame is Nevin Nollop, author of the sentence: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. 
 Nollop is very proud of Nevin. So much so, that they have erected a statue in his honor with his famous sentence set in tiles around the statue. But, what would happen if those tiles began to fall off their pedestal? Would the statue merely need some maintenance to make sure other letters do not fall? Or, is it a sign from the great Nevin Nollop that the fallen letters are no longer worthy of use? 
 Of course, any decent person would realize that the latter is exactly what is meant by this phenomenon. And if the letters are not worthy, well then, they just need to be outlawed. 
 Watch, and try to read, as the written word is destroyed in front of your very eyes. The book begins with long beautiful letters to and from friends and family members. By the end, when only "LMNOP" are the only legal letters left, the letters become similar to a txt msg I rcvd 2day. 
 Ella Minnow Pea is a quirky little book that is both hilarious and poignant. It is a fabulous read that word lovers with thoroughly enjoy. 
 *For the record: I wrote this review out long hand, on paper, with a pen, before typing it into my computer. Insert smiley face emoticon here.

For the longest time I've avoided these books because... well... look at the covers. If that doesn't scream cheesy paranormal romance I don't know what will. But after so many people raving about this series, I decided why not at least give the first one a try. I was COMPLETELY blown away; it's definitely the first angel demon story I've even felt like was plausible and I was able to suspend my disbelief and enjoy.

I remember back when I picked up the first volume of Outcast. I was just starting to get in to reading comics and graphic novels and I picked it up on a whim based on its description alone. I didn't even realize that it was written by Robert Kirkman, creator of the uber successful The Walking Dead series until the cashier brought it up. 
 I definitely had some high hopes going into this second volume as the first moved at a rather slow pace and felt like more of a set up or an introduction to a much larger story. I remember feeling like it definitely had potential after reading it and that volume two would probably dive deeper into the story. 
 Unfortunately, the first half of volume two still moved at a rather slow pace. It felt repetitive as Kyle and Reverend Anderson continue to visit those who may be possessed and yet no answers are given as to what kind of power it is that Kyle has over these possessed humans. I know that it is likely that the intention of the story is to unravel the answers slowly and to have some sort of big reveal, but each of the scenarios in which Kyle and the Reverend meet with those who are possessed feels like a cookie cutter copy of one another. 
 However, as much as I was starting to feel deterred, things turned around for the better about half way through this second volume. The story finally started to pick up and I found myself interested again. I couldn't help but feel for Kyle as he finally interacts with his wife and daughter again. And then of course, there's the fantastic ending to this volume that has me wanting the next issue as soon as possible. Honestly, I wasn't expecting that ending at all! 
 Although the story definitely picked up towards the end, I'm still hoping for more from the next volume. This story has the potential to be great and I really do hope that we get some solid answers in the future and maybe a little more action. Outcast is still as dark as ever and I can see the story becoming even darker in the future. 
 What I love about the art within this series is the little hints of neon colouring. The front cover of this particular volume definitely demonstrates the kind of colouring that you can expect to find within. 
 Although I was a little skeptical while reading the first half of this volume, I'm still eager to find out where this story will go in the future. I'm also quite excited to see how they work this all in to the future television adaptation!

I read two short novels this week, The Ocean at the End of the Lane, by Neil Gaiman, and this one, Blood on Snow, by Jo Nesbo. Both are very good writers, but these two short books reconfirmed that I'm a mystery reader, not a fantasy reader. I vastly preferred Nesbo's book to Gaiman's, although I admire Gaiman's writing. 
 Set in late 1976, Blood on Snow is exceedingly noir, reminding me of Raymond Chandler, complete with femme fatale, but it also features an unbelievably sympathetic killer-with-a-heart-of-gold, named Olav. I was reminded of the film The Professional, with Jean Reno and a young Natalie Portman. Like Reno's Leon, Olav is sad, lonely, and damaged. But unlike Leon, who is changed by his relationship with 12-year-old Mathilda, Olav has been providing for the helpless and the victimized since he began his relatively short career as a Norwegian hitman. After trying a variety of criminal roles, Olav discovers that he has a knack for assassination. He yearns for love, but that's hard to find in his world. He sublimates these feelings by doing good works. Olav's life turns a hard turn when he decides not to "fix" his boss's wife Corina, who is having a destructive affair with a younger man. Instead, he decides to save her. Olav is so heartbreakingly vulnerable: "I held her incredibly carefully like one of the dried flowers I sometimes found in the pages of books from the library, so brittle and fragile that they dissolved under my fingers as soon as I touched them. I was scared she would disappear" (page 87). He has the soul of a poet trapped in the body of a killer. 
 I have read Nesbo's Harry Hole books, but I actually prefer this one. It's a little too short, but I liked the pace of Nesbo's narrative. I felt that I immediately knew Olav. Nesbo delineates the character with quick brushstrokes. You sense right away that he's doomed. You hope that you are wrong but when he hooks up with Corina instead of Maria, you get a very bad feeling. Olav lives in a very cold place, in more ways than one.

Like the humanity it portrays Cormac McCarthy's prose in 'The Road' is pared down to it's core, teeth bared with a vicious depiction of humanity. His words are careful and full, hinting at far more then they ever reveal. Anonymous disasters past and present hound the unnamed narrator and his son as they journey along the deserted highways of America, past the last dregs of a society long drained of its humanity. Mad Max without the hero, apocalypse without the bang, a study of character in the face of nothing. 
 These features make the book as sparse and barren as the landscape it's describing. I found it difficult to become invested in the fate of characters who were having trouble investing in themselves. The progress is hazy, and the victories hollow, like shells of people traveling forward due to a lack of friction rather then any particular drive. Hopelessness in all it's glory. 
 The book ends on an up, a minor victory, which is slightly disconcerting. It seems contrary to the world being created, the used up nature of everything else encountered, too hopeful and incongruous. Like a felt tail pinned to a picture of a donkey, it may fit but it doesn't really belong. Death was expected, inevitable, required, but the hope seems like a prayer in a book that long ago declared god dead, a turning on itself to find something that it didn't bother to construct. I enjoyed the text, found things worth pondering, loved the descriptions, but I do not think it's untouchable. It's too inhuman to love as a piece of sentimental literature, but too hopeful to realize genuine despondancy.

Defending Jacob isn't my normal kind of book. It's a crime thriller, and I just don't often get around to that genre. I picked it up for my mom, and I'm not even sure why I started reading it, but a day after finishing (to say something about it, I finished it in one day in three giant chunks) I'm still thinking about it. 
 Andrew Barber is the First Assistant DA in his upper class, educated, small-town, good place to grow up in, community. The murder of a 14 year old boy rocks the town, and Andy, knowing this will be a high-profile case, decides to take it on. He is then called off the case when the primary suspect emerges: his own 14 year old son Jacob. Soon, everything Andy knows about his son is called into question, except that for Andy, Jacob is forever innocent. 
 A majority of Defending Jacob is good. Jacob isn't the sweet Boy Scout type (a fact Andy only begins to understand). He owns a knife, his internet posts are suspicious, accounts from his friends show him to be moody, mean sometimes, mysterious, and with a definite grudge against the deceased boy. This is a smart choice on Landy's side--for one, the reader doesn't automatically side with Jacob. This isn't a clear cut trial. Just as soon as Jacob may seem innocent, something else emerges that makes you question everything. Secondly, while Jacob's flaws are exposed to the reader and Andy, Andy's steadfast belief in his son is only more highlighted. Andy is not a naive man, but he is a father who loves his son and may have a giant blind spot where Jacob is concerned. 
 Because Landay's spent time in the legal field, the courtroom scenes are written well. I found myself able to see the courtroom and the trial as it unfolded. Done less effectively for me is the talk about genetics and how it plays into the defense/prosecution. The prosecuting attorney is portrayed as the villain, and because this is in Andy's point of view I get it, but he seems a bit too 'mustache twirling' for my liking. 
 Keep reading until the end. Just when you thought you knew how it will go, it'll throw you.

 I've only read one other Keri Arthur book, but she has a tendency to shove everything and the kitchen sink into a story and make it work. This book is no different. It's one part paranormal romance, one part urban fantasy, one part science fiction, and one part dystopia. It should basically be a mess, but this book is anything but that. 
 Tig is a dechet, a lab-grown super-soldier made to fight in a war years earlier. She lives in the bones of her old bunker, everyone else eradicated by the shifters during the war. The bunker is full of ghosts that she can talk to, children ghosts that follow her around. Despite being a hermit, she's thrown into the middle of a plot where people are stealing children and, as a big ol' softie, she risks life and limb to try and save them. That and people threaten her ghosts, which isn't cool. 
 Teaming up with shifters who are wary of her existence and her nature, she uses all her powers to find out who's behind the kidnappings. Along the way she meets up with an old lover, and they pick up their fling where they left off. She's also quite smitten with the shifter she regularly runs missions with, but he's not at all trustworthy of her. 
 The vampires in this series are pretty gross, and I thank the author for going that direction with them. They swarm and become insubstantial. They devour and smell bad. Honestly, they were pretty terrifying. 
 I picked this book up and I didn't set it down. I loved every minute of it and I can't wait to pick up the next installment. I especially loved the little children ghosts. They were unsettlingly cute, and helped get Tig out of a few tough scrapes. 
 Tig's background is intense and Keri Arthur does a great job explaining it in bits and pieces without the entire history being an infodump or slog. I appreciate that. Not many authors can throw such a mishmash of things together and keep the plot moving at such a pace. 
 There is one thing that threw me out of the narrative for awhile. Tig's old romantic partner was a special breed of assassin called the, and I'm not making this up, Blue Steel Project. 
 Oops. I dunno if Keri Arthur just never saw Zoolander or if she did and was doing a subtle nod at it, but a salamander-humanoid assassin, Blue Steel class? I died a little on the inside. I had to take like a thirty minute break and yet I still somehow finished the book in a day. 
 Anyway, great book. Great characters. Would recommend. Now it's time for me to go start the second and hope upon hope it doesn't suffer from second book syndrome.

This seems like a good candidate for so many of my usual tags--horror, fantasy, specfic... Wright's book is chock-full of minute detail, including some details so bizarre that they're hard to process. In some ways Scientology is very like any other cult (pardon me, "new religious movement.") It has leaders who enjoy exceptional wealth while the majority of its members labor in penury. It isolates its members from their families and friends, and seeks to control their financial, personal, social, and psychological lives. It's said to hold some of its members in physical gaol, where they're subject to physical and mental abuse as well as near-starvation conditions. This is all pretty familiar stuff from Jim Jones, Waco, the Rajneeshi, and a ton of other coercive spiritual movements. 
 But Scientology is especially interesting in its symbiotic relationship with Hollywood and the cult of celebrity. When you think about it, the star factory is an ideal partner for a fringe religion. It's the locus of fabulous riches, insecure and idealistic personalities, fast deals, and constantly shifting norms. What does any cult need to thrive? People, preferably wealthy and impressionable. What do aspiring film stars need? Connections, relationships, a way in. Scientology took advantage of this opportunity early on, and positioned itself as a leg up for actors, directors, writers, and others trying to break into a very tough business. It's not hard to see why so many people, caught up in the ego-slamming whirlwind of Hollywood, would be grateful to clamber aboard the good ship L. Ron Hubbard. And it's not hard to see what Scientology gains from charging people thousands of dollars for auditing and courses, or from associating itself with influential, popular, high-access people like Tom Cruise and John Travolta. 
 Still, it can be a little tough to live in the Scientology mindset for the four hundred fifty-odd pages of this book. My hat is off to Wright. By the time I was finished reading about the constant bullying, paranoia, psychopathy, abuse, delusion, and greed of the Scientology set, I was feeling pretty sick. I admire him for taking on the topic, not only because it's so glum but because Scientology is famous for mercilessly persecuting its critics, in ways both legal and illegal. 
 And I admire him even more for coming to the conclusion that many if not most people don't join Scientology because they're dumb or greedy. Most join because they believe it holds the key to making the world a better place. They're idealistic and they have good intentions--they buy into the rhetoric telling them that if they can go clear, they won't just better their own lives, they'll improve the world as a whole. It's hard not to get a little more depressed at the thought of just how wrong they are.
